item.who: Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), Belgium and Italy, and the artists who drew his book
item.idea: In 1543 Vesalius published a huge book about the human body, 'De humani corporis fabrica' (On the Fabric of the Human Body). He had looked inside human bodies himself and showed that the famous Greek doctor Galen had made mistakes, because Galen had mostly studied animals such as monkeys.
item.then: Some doctors were angry: Galen had been trusted for about 1,300 years. Vesalius's own teacher Jacobus Sylvius attacked him.
item.now: Vesalius was right, and his book changed medicine. Its wonderful drawings were made by artists, probably from the workshop of the painter Titian; one may have been Jan van Calcar. Their names are not on the pictures, so we cannot be sure who drew them.
item.ask: The drawings made the book famous, but we don't know for sure who drew them. Should the artist's name be on the book too?

item.who: Jane Goodall (1934–2025), England, working in Tanzania
item.idea: In 1960, without a university degree, Goodall began watching chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania. She sat quietly for years until the chimps trusted her. She saw that chimp mothers carry, feed, play with and teach their babies for years, that young chimps learn by watching, and that each chimp has their own character.
item.then: Some scientists criticised her for giving the chimps names instead of numbers and for saying they had feelings and personalities.
item.now: Her findings are accepted; long childhoods and learning from mothers are now known in chimps, elephants, whales and many birds. Scientists still discuss how to study animal feelings carefully.
item.ask: Jane gave the chimps names, like Flo and David Greybeard. Some scientists said that was not scientific. What do you think? Does naming an animal help you see them better, or make you see what you want to see?

item.who: Jean-Henri Fabre (1823–1915), France
item.idea: Fabre was a schoolteacher who watched insects in fields and later in his own garden, which he called the Harmas. He found out how wasps, beetles and spiders really live by watching them where they live. He wrote ten books about them in plain, lively words.
item.then: Some university scientists looked down on him for writing so simply, as if easy words meant easy science. Fabre also did not accept Charles Darwin's idea that living things change over very long times. The two wrote to each other politely about it.
item.now: His watching of insect lives is still admired. On evolution, the evidence has gone firmly against him: Darwin was right that living things change over time. A person can be a careful watcher and still be wrong about a big idea.
item.ask: Fabre was right about wasps but wrong about evolution. Can someone be a good scientist and still be wrong sometimes? How do we find out which parts are right?

lessons.title: How do we know? Finding out by noticing and testing

item.title: Oops paintings
steps: Drop a blob or two of paint in the middle of a sheet.
Fold the paper in half, press, and open it.
Look at the accidental shape. What does it remind you of?
Add eyes, legs, words or colour to turn it into something.
Give it a name and say one thing you noticed that you didn't plan.
item.outcome: A painting made from an accident, and the idea that noticing turns an accident into a discovery.

item.title: The continent jigsaw
steps: Find South America and Africa on the map.
Cut them out along the coast.
Slide them across the paper towards each other. Do they fit?
Look for other pieces that might fit.
Ask: 'If they fitted together long ago, what must have happened?'
item.outcome: A map puzzle showing the clue that made Alfred Wegener think the continents had moved.

item.who: Alfred Wegener (1880–1930), Germany
item.idea: In 1912 Wegener said the continents were once joined in one giant land and have slowly drifted apart. His evidence: the coasts of Africa and South America fit, the same fossils and rocks are found on both sides of the ocean, and coal is found in icy Antarctica.
item.then: Most geologists laughed. He could not explain what force could push whole continents, and he was a weather scientist, not a geologist.
item.now: In the 1950s and 1960s, maps of the ocean floor (made with the help of Marie Tharp) and other evidence showed that the Earth's crust is made of plates that move a few centimetres a year. Wegener was mostly right. He died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930, before he was believed.
item.ask: Wegener had good clues but no explanation of how. Were the other scientists wrong to doubt him? What would have convinced you?

item.title: Beautiful Oops!
item.author: Barney Saltzberg
item.why: A lift-the-flap book that turns spills and tears into new things, to go with the Oops paintings.

steps: Knock each object gently.
Describe its sound: ring, chime, tok, clack, or almost nothing.
Find which material absorbs sound best.
Make a family rhythm.
Muffle a phone alarm with steel and then cloth.
item.outcome: Your child hears that materials make different sounds, and that soft materials absorb sound.

item.who: The rubber makers of ancient Mexico and Central America, and the archaeologists Dorothy Hosler and Michael Tarkanian (MIT, 1999)
item.idea: More than 3,000 years ago, people in Mesoamerica (such as the Olmec) mixed latex, the milky sap of the rubber tree, with juice from a morning glory vine. This made rubber bouncy and strong enough for balls, sandals and bands. Hosler and Tarkanian tested the recipe in the lab and showed it really works.
item.then: For a long time the 'invention' of useful rubber was credited mainly to Charles Goodyear in the USA, who found in 1839 that heating rubber with sulphur made it strong. The older Mesoamerican knowledge was hardly mentioned.
item.now: Historians and chemists now accept that Mesoamerican peoples processed rubber thousands of years before Goodyear, with a different method. Goodyear's method is the one industry uses.
item.ask: If someone did something first but didn't write it in a book, did they still discover it? How could we find out what they knew?

item.who: Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law (2017), USA
item.idea: They counted all the plastic made in the world since about 1950 and estimated that only about 9 out of every 100 parts of plastic waste had been recycled. Most had been buried in landfills or had ended up in the land and sea.
item.then: Many people had believed that putting plastic in the recycling bin solved the problem.
item.now: Scientists broadly agree that recycling alone cannot keep up. People still debate the best answer: better recycling, using less plastic, reusing things, or new materials.
item.ask: If only a few bottles out of every hundred get recycled, what else could we do? Which idea do you think would work best, and how could we check?

item.title: One Plastic Bag: Isatou Ceesay and the Recycling Women of the Gambia
item.author: Miranda Paul
item.why: A true story of women who turned plastic rubbish into purses: materials, reuse and who does the work.

lessons.title: Me and others: how people are alike and how each one is different

item: one part of how a person looks or is, like height, hair or the hand they write with
how far it is from the tip of one middle finger to the other, with arms stretched out wide
one person or one animal, different from every other one

item.who: Jane Goodall (1934–2025), England, scientist who studied chimpanzees
item.idea: In 1960 Goodall began watching wild chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania. She gave each one a name and wrote about each one's own way of behaving. She saw a chimpanzee she named David Greybeard use grass stems to fish termites out of a mound.
item.then: Some scientists said she should give the animals numbers, not names, and that talking about an animal's personality and feelings was not science. Many were also surprised that an animal other than humans made and used tools.
item.now: Scientists now agree that chimpanzees, and many other animals, have their own personalities and feelings, and that each one is an individual. Tool use has been seen in many animals, including crows.
item.ask: Why might a number make it easier to forget that a chimpanzee has feelings? What would you need to see to know an animal is feeling happy?

item.who: K. Ullas Karanth (born 1948), Karnataka, India, tiger scientist
item.idea: In the 1990s, in Nagarahole forest in Karnataka, Karanth set up camera traps: cameras that take a photo when an animal walks past. Because each tiger's stripes are different, he could tell from the photos which tiger was which, and count how many tigers lived there.
item.then: Before this, tigers were often counted from their pawprints, which is much less reliable, because pawprints of different tigers can look alike.
item.now: Counting tigers with camera traps and their stripe patterns is now used across India and other countries.
item.ask: Why are stripes better than pawprints for telling tigers apart? What makes you different from everyone else in a way a camera could see?

item.who: Paul Ekman, USA, psychologist, and Lisa Feldman Barrett (born 1963), USA, psychologist
item.idea: From the 1960s, Ekman showed photos of faces to people in many countries, including people in Papua New Guinea who had seen few outsiders. He said six feelings (happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised and disgusted) show on faces the same way everywhere. Barrett and others later tested people in different places in a different way, and found that people often do not read faces the same way, and that one person's anger can look very different from another's.
item.then: Ekman's idea became very popular, and many books and computer programs were built on it.
item.now: Scientists still argue. Many agree that some face signals are common across people. Many also agree that faces alone do not reliably tell you what someone feels, and that you need to know the person and what is happening.
item.ask: If someone is smiling, are they always happy? What else could you look at, or ask, to find out?

item.title: The Visitor under Kavya's Bed
text: I am the one who lives under Kavya's bed. I have two curly horns, a coat of thick blue fur, and long claws on every finger. I do not eat children. I eat dust, mostly, and sometimes a lost biscuit.

Kavya lives in a flat in Madurai, on the fourth floor. Every night her Amma reads her a story, switches on the little night lamp, and looks under the bed. Amma always looks right at me. She never sees me. Grown-ups usually don't.

That night the fan was going round and round, and the jasmine in the window smelled sweet. Kavya's eyes were almost shut. I had been alone under that bed for a very long time. So I did something I had never done before. I came out.
I climbed up slowly, one claw at a time. I sat on the end of the bed. The bed went 'creak'.
Kavya opened her eyes. She saw my horns. She saw my claws. She pulled the sheet up to her nose.
'Go away!' she said. Her voice was a squeak. 'You are a monster!'
'I only wanted to say hello,' I said.
'You have horns,' said Kavya. 'And claws. Things with claws are scary.'
I looked down at my claws. I had never thought of them as scary. They were just my hands. I use them to dig in the dust and to scratch my ears.
'I don't hurt anyone with them,' I said. 'This is just how I look.'
Kavya did not answer. She was looking at my hands. They were shaking. I tried to keep them still, but they would not stop.
'Why are your hands shaking?' she asked.
I did not want to tell her. But it was the truth. 'Because I am scared,' I said. 'You are much bigger than me. And you shouted.'
Kavya let the sheet slip down a little. 'You are scared of me?'
'Yes,' I said. 'When I am scared, my heart beats very fast. And I want to hide.'
'Mine too,' said Kavya slowly. 'My heart is beating fast right now.' She put her hand on her chest. Then she looked at me again, more carefully this time, the way you look at something new.
'You have two eyes,' she said. 'Like me.'
'And two ears,' I said, and wiggled them.

'I have ten fingers,' said Kavya, holding up her hands. I held up mine. 'Ten,' I said. Mine had claws on the end, and hers had small pink nails. But when we put our hands side by side, they were almost the same size.
'Are you hungry?' she asked. 'People get hungry at night sometimes.'
'Very,' I said. She reached under her pillow and found half a biscuit she was not supposed to have. She broke it in two and gave me the bigger piece.

We ate our biscuit pieces in the light of the night lamp. Kavya told me she was scared of the dark, and of the dog on the ground floor, and of the dentist. I told her I was scared of the broom, and of the loud pressure cooker, and of being alone.
'I am scared of being alone too,' said Kavya. 'That is why I like the night lamp.'
We sat for a while without saying anything. The fan went round. A scooter passed on the road below.
'Will you come out again tomorrow?' she asked.
'If you won't shout,' I said.
'I won't,' said Kavya. 'Now I know what you look like. And I know what you are like. Those are not the same thing.'
In the morning, Amma came in and looked under the bed, the way she always does. Kavya leaned over the side and waved at me. Amma looked where she was waving and saw only dust.
'Who are you waving at?' asked Amma.
'My friend,' said Kavya. 'He has horns. And he is scared of the pressure cooker, just like my little brother.'
item.epiphany: For the parent: the visitor looks completely different from Kavya, with horns, fur and claws. The story turns when Kavya sees his hands shaking and finds he is scared too. After that she notices how alike they are: two eyes, ten fingers, hungry at night, scared of being alone. What someone looks like does not tell you what they are like inside, and the feelings inside are often the same.
ask: Why was Kavya scared at first?
Why were the visitor's hands shaking?
Name three ways Kavya and the visitor were similar.
Name two ways they were different.
Kavya says, 'Now I know what you look like. And I know what you are like.' What is the difference?

lessons.title: Patterns and symmetry: the same on both sides

item.title: Two handprints
item.question: Are your two hands the same, or a flipped pair?
steps: Your child puts the left hand flat on a paper, fingers spread. Draw round it.
Do the same with the right hand on the second paper.
Cut out both hand shapes.
Lay both shapes drawn side up and put one on top of the other.
Now flip one shape over and put it on top again.
item.predict: Ask: 'Will the two hands match when we put one on top of the other?'
item.observe: Laid the same way up, the thumbs point opposite ways and the hands do not match. Flipped, they nearly match. Small differences in finger length or width are normal.
item.why: Our left and right hands are mirror images: each is the other one flipped. That is why they match only after one is flipped over. They are not exactly the same, because each hand grows a little differently and the one we use more is often a little bigger.
item.safety: Use safe scissors. A grown-up cuts round the fingers if needed.

item.title: Balance pose
steps: Stand in mountain pose: feet together, arms by your sides, standing tall.
Check: is your body the same on both sides?
Stand on your left leg in tree pose. Put your right foot on the inside of your left leg and join your hands at your chest.
Count to five slowly. Then swap legs.
Talk about which side was harder.
item.outcome: The child feels that the body looks the same on both sides but is not exactly the same.

item.title: Rhythm and mirror dance
steps: Put a hand on your chest and feel the heartbeat.
Clap a rhythm together: clap, clap, rest, clap, clap, rest.
Stand facing each other and play a song.
The leader moves slowly. The other person copies like a mirror: the leader's right arm is the mirror's left arm.
Swap who leads.
item.outcome: The child hears a pattern in time and feels what a mirror image is with the whole body.

item.who: Wilson Bentley (1865–1931), a farmer in Vermont, United States
item.idea: Wilson Bentley joined a camera to a microscope and, in 1885, became the first person known to photograph a single snowflake. Over his life he photographed more than 5,000 snowflakes. They showed that each snowflake has six arms or six sides, and that big snowflakes differ from each other in many small ways.
item.then: Many of his neighbours thought it was a waste of time for a farmer to spend snowy days looking at snowflakes. He sold copies of his photos for very little money.
item.now: His photos are still famous and still used. Scientists agree that snow crystals have six sides because of how water particles join together when they freeze.
item.ask: People laughed at Wilson Bentley for looking closely at snowflakes. What small thing at home would you like to look at closely for a long time?

item.who: Gift Siromoney, Rani Siromoney and Kamala Krithivasan, scientists in Chennai who worked on mathematics and computers
item.idea: In the 1970s, these three scientists studied kolams drawn in Tamil Nadu. They showed that many kolam patterns follow exact rules, of the same kind that computer scientists use to describe pictures and languages.
item.then: Kolams were mostly seen as women's daily art, not as mathematics. Their work showed that the patterns hold real mathematical rules.
item.now: Mathematicians and computer scientists around the world still study kolams. The rules were found in kolams that women had drawn from memory, and taught to their daughters, for hundreds of years.
item.ask: Is a woman who draws a kolam every morning doing mathematics, even if nobody calls her a mathematician? Why do you think so?

lessons.title: Plants: their parts, and how they grow towards light

item.title: The shoebox maze
item.question: Can a bean shoot find the way to the light through a maze?
need: two pieces of cardboard and tape
steps: Cut a hole about the size of a ₹10 coin in one short end of the box, near the top.
Tape two pieces of cardboard inside as shelves, one from the left and one from the right, to make a zigzag path.
Plant the sprouted bean in the cup of soil and put the cup at the bottom of the box, far from the hole.
Close the lid and stand the box with the hole facing a sunny window.
Every two days, water the bean a little and close the lid again quickly.
item.predict: Ask: 'Will the bean find the hole? Which way will the shoot grow? Why?'
item.observe: Draw the shoot each time you check. Note which way the shoot is turning.
item.why: Plants sense light with special proteins, mostly near the growing tip of the shoot. The shoot grows faster on the shaded side, so the shoot bends towards the light. The bean's shoot turns round each shelf until they reach the hole.

lessons.title: How a seed sprouts and grows into a plant

item.who: Monica Gagliano and colleagues, University of Western Australia (study published in 2017)
item.idea: They grew pea seedlings in Y-shaped pots. When water ran through a pipe under one arm (so the soil stayed dry, but the sound of water was there), more roots grew towards that side. They suggested roots may 'hear' water.
item.then: Some scientists found the study exciting. Others said one study is not enough, and that something other than sound might explain it.
item.now: Roots certainly sense moisture and grow towards it. Whether they really use sound is still being tested and argued about.
item.ask: What would you need to see, again and again, before you believed that roots can hear?

lessons.title: Our senses: how we find out about the world

item.title: Bhulu and the Smell of Tuktuki
text: My name is Bhulu. The humans gave it to me. It means something like 'the one who forgets', which is unfair, because I forget nothing. I am a dog of Ballygunge, in Kolkata, brown with a white tip on my tail and a torn left ear from a fight I did not start, and I know every smell between the sweet shop and the tram line.

You live in a world of colours. I live in a world of smells. When I walk down our lane in the morning, my nose reads it like a newspaper. The milkman passed at five, his cycle smelling of rubber and cows. The cat from number twelve sat on that wall for a long time, feeling cross. The fish-seller's basket dripped here, and here, and here. A new puppy went by, frightened, keeping close to his mother. I can smell who was here yesterday. I can smell whether they were happy.
And every afternoon at four, I can smell Tuktuki.

Tuktuki is five, and she lives on the second floor of the yellow house. She smells of coconut oil in her hair, of Marie biscuits, of the soap her grandmother buys from the market, and of something underneath all that which is only Tuktuki and nobody else in the whole world. Every afternoon she comes down with half a biscuit hidden in her fist, and she squats and holds it out, and I take it very gently, so as not to touch her fingers with my teeth. Then she strokes my torn ear and says, “Poor Bhulu,” though it does not hurt any more.

In autumn, the city goes mad with Durga Puja. Huge bamboo pandals go up on every corner, with goddesses inside taller than houses, and for five nights the streets are full of drums and lights and more people than there are smells. It is the hardest week of the year for a dog's nose. Incense, frying luchis, flowers by the cartload, the sweat of a hundred thousand people, the smoke of the dhunuchi dance. My nose is so full I can barely think.
On the eighth night, Tuktuki got lost.

I saw her family go past at the start of the evening, all in new clothes, the father carrying the baby, the grandmother holding Tuktuki's hand. Tuktuki was in a shining green dress I had never seen, and her face was painted with a little red dot and white spots over her eyebrows, like the goddess. I did not know her at first by looking. To my eyes she was just one more small shining human in a crowd of shining humans.

Later, when the crowd at the big pandal was so thick it moved like a river, I heard the grandmother calling. “Tuktuki! Tuktuki!” Her voice was high and thin and frightened. Then the father, louder. Then a policeman with a whistle.

I went to the grandmother. I sniffed her hand, the one that had been holding Tuktuki's hand all evening. And there it was, under the incense and the flowers and the frying: coconut oil, Marie biscuit, and the something that is only Tuktuki.
I put my nose down and I ran.

Humans think a crowd is a wall. To my nose a crowd is a forest with paths through it, and every person leaves a path of smell behind them, like a thread. I found Tuktuki's thread at the edge of the pandal, where the grandmother's hand had let go. It was thin, and it was trampled by a thousand feet, and twice I lost it in a cloud of incense and had to go back and find it again. It went past the balloon man, behind the sweet stall, round the back of the pandal where the generators hum, and under a table covered with a cloth.
Under the table it was dark. A small person was curled up there in a green dress, crying without any noise.
I could not see her well. My eyes are not good in the dark, and she did not look like Tuktuki. But my nose said, very clearly, Tuktuki, Tuktuki, Tuktuki.
I whined. She went still. She could not see me either, there in the dark, only a shape. A big dark shape with teeth could be anything. She shrank back.
So I crept close and put my head down by her hand, and I waited.
Her fingers came out, slowly, and touched my head. They found the soft fur between my eyes. They moved to the left. They found my ear, and the place where it is torn.
“Bhulu?” she whispered.
She knew me by her fingers, the way I knew her by my nose.

She held on to my neck, and I walked her out from under the table, very slowly, through the river of people, following my own path back. I heard the grandmother before I saw her, and the grandmother heard Tuktuki before she saw her, and then there was a great deal of noise and crying and hugging, and somebody gave me a whole packet of Marie biscuits, which I did not deserve but ate anyway.

Now, every afternoon at four, Tuktuki comes down with a biscuit and strokes my ear. Sometimes she shuts her eyes and sniffs the air very hard, and says, “Bhulu, what can you smell?” And I wish I could tell her: everything. Everything that was ever here.
item.epiphany: Different animals know the world through different senses. In festival clothes and in the dark, Bhulu cannot recognise Tuktuki by sight, but he follows her smell through the crowd. Tuktuki cannot see Bhulu either, but she knows him by touch, by his torn ear. The turn is the moment under the table when neither can see and both still know each other.
ask: How did Bhulu find Tuktuki in a crowd of thousands?
Why did Bhulu not know Tuktuki by looking at her?
How did Tuktuki know it was Bhulu in the dark?
Bhulu says he lives in a world of smells. What world do you live in?
What do you think Bhulu could smell at the end that Tuktuki could not?

lessons.title: Sound: where it comes from and how it reaches our ears

item.who: Robert Boyle (1627–1691) and Robert Hooke (1635–1703), England
item.idea: In 1660 Boyle reported putting a ticking watch inside a glass jar and pumping the air out. The ticking grew fainter and fainter, and came back when air was let in. The air pump that made this possible was built by his assistant, Robert Hooke.
item.then: In the 1640s in Rome, Gasparo Berti rang a bell inside a tube with the air taken out, and still heard it. Athanasius Kircher, who wrote about the test, said that sound does not need air. The sound had probably escaped through the metal that held the bell, and some air may have been left inside. Boyle's careful test convinced most people that sound needs air, or something else, to travel through.
item.now: It is accepted: sound needs something to travel through (air, water, wood). In empty space there is no sound. Hooke, the skilled builder whose pump made the test possible, became a great scientist himself but is often left out of the story.
item.ask: Kircher said one thing and Boyle said the opposite. Why might two careful people get different results? What would you need to check?

item.who: Itzhak Khait, Lilach Hadany and colleagues, Tel Aviv University, Israel (published 2023)
item.idea: They put tomato and tobacco plants in quiet boxes with special microphones. They recorded tiny clicks, too high for people to hear. The plants clicked far more often when they were thirsty or when their stems were cut. A computer could tell a thirsty plant from a cut one by their clicks.
item.then: Many scientists were amazed. Others pointed out that the clicks are probably caused by tiny air bubbles in the plant's water tubes, so the plant may not be 'talking' on purpose.
item.now: The recordings are accepted, but what they mean is debated. Nobody knows yet whether any animal, such as a moth looking for a healthy plant to lay eggs on, actually listens to them.
item.ask: If a plant clicks without meaning to, could the click still tell an animal something? What experiment would show whether a moth listens?

item.who: John Marzluff, University of Washington, USA (living)
item.idea: Marzluff and his team wore a scary rubber mask while they caught some wild crows, measured them and let them go unhurt. Then they walked past in the mask on other days.
item.then: Many people thought birds could not tell one person from another.
item.now: For years after, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask, but not at people in other masks. Even young crows who had never been caught learned to scold the mask, from older crows. Scientists agree that crows remember faces and teach each other.
item.ask: How did the young crows know the mask was dangerous, when it had never caught them?

nature reserves, sanctuaries and sacred groves

item.title: Water bowl and bug hotel
need: a cut plastic bottle or old tin
dry sticks, rolled cardboard, dry leaves, bark
steps: Put the dish in a shady, quiet place. Fill it 2 to 3 cm deep, with a stone in the middle so small birds and bees can stand.
Change the water every day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it.
Pack the bottle or tin tightly with sticks, cardboard, leaves and bark.
Lay it on its side in a quiet corner.
Check every day and draw any visitors.
item.outcome: Two new homes or helps for small creatures, and a list of visitors.

item.title: Our tiny nature reserve
steps: Choose a corner of a balcony, window ledge, school or building: one square metre is enough.
Draw a plan with the water bowl, the bug hotel, plants and a sign.
Give it a name and one rule (for example: no sweeping away the dead leaves, no spraying poison).
Plant something for bees and butterflies, like tulsi, marigold or ixora.
Keep a two-week care chart: Watered? Who visited?
Show the family and the neighbours who came.
item.outcome: A small protected corner with a plan, a sign and a list of visitors.

item.who: Wangari Maathai (1940–2011), Kenya
item.idea: Wangari Maathai was a scientist who studied animals' bodies. She saw that women in the Kenyan countryside walked further and further for firewood and water, because the trees had been cut. In 1977 she started the Green Belt Movement. Village women were paid a little for each young tree they grew and planted. Together they planted tens of millions of trees.
item.then: Many powerful men laughed at her or called her a troublemaker. She was arrested more than once for protecting forests and parks from being built on.
item.now: Accepted. In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Scientists agree that planting the right trees in the right places can bring back water and soil.
item.ask: Wangari said each person can do 'the little thing' they can. Hers was planting trees. What little thing could you do for the place where you live?

item.who: Jadav 'Molai' Payeng (born around 1963), Assam, India
item.idea: In 1979, when he was a teenager, Jadav Payeng found many snakes dead from the heat on a bare sandbank in the Brahmaputra river in Assam. There was no shade. He began to plant bamboo, and then trees, and kept planting almost every day for decades. His forest, now called Molai forest, covers hundreds of hectares. Deer, rhinos, tigers and elephants visit it.
item.then: For years almost nobody knew. In 2008, forest officers following a herd of elephants were amazed to find a whole forest there.
item.now: Accepted. In 2015 he received the Padma Shri. His forest shows how a bare place can become a habitat again, though it takes many years.
item.ask: The snakes died because the sandbank had no shade. What other things does a forest give to animals? How could you check that the animals really came back?

item.title: Chirri Needs a Hole
text: My name is Chirri, and I am a house sparrow. I am small and brown, with a grey cap and a black bib on my chest. I live in Madurai, in a lane full of cycle bells, pressure cookers and the smell of frying vadas.

All my life I lived in a hole. Not just any hole: the best hole in the whole lane, under the old clay tiles of Nila's grandmother's house, just where the roof met the wall. It was dark and dry and just my size. Every year my wife and I filled it with straw, threads and feathers, and every year we had chicks, three or four of them, cheeping in the dark.
Then, one winter, the old house was knocked down.

I watched from the electric wire. Workers came with hammers. The tiles came down. My hole came down. In its place they built a new house of smooth grey concrete with big glass windows. It was very clean. It had no holes at all.

When it was time to nest, my wife and I flew round and round the new house. Smooth wall. Smooth wall. Glass. Smooth wall. There was nowhere. We tried the next house. Smooth. The next. Smooth. Behind the bakery the old tin roof had a gap, but the pigeons had got there first.

Nila saw me. Nila is seven, she has a gap in her teeth, and she notices things. She saw me sitting on her window grill, looking sad (sparrows can be sad, whatever people say). 'Amma,' she said, 'that sparrow is hungry.'
So Nila put out bread.
It was kind of her. I ate a little. But I wasn't hungry, not really. I needed a hole.
The next day Nila put out more bread. And a biscuit. And some murukku. The crows came and ate it all, and squabbled, and made a mess on the balcony. Nila's father sighed.

Then my wife found a place. It was a dark grey box on the wall by the gate, with a little gap at the bottom where the wires came in. It was dark and dry and just our size. We started to carry straw into it.

Nila's father saw us and shouted. 'Not there! That's the electric meter!' He was worried, not angry. He blocked the gap with tape. It was the right thing to do, because a meter box is dangerous for birds. But where were we to go now?

That evening Nila sat on the step with her chin on her knees and watched me. She didn't put out bread. She just watched. She watched me fly to the corner of the yard where nobody went, where the grass was long and there was a tangle of what her father called weeds. She watched me come out with something green and wriggling in my beak.
'Amma,' she said, 'what is the sparrow eating?'
Her mother looked. 'A caterpillar, I think.'
'Not bread?'
'Baby sparrows can't eat bread,' her mother said slowly. 'I remember now. Your Paati used to say it. They need soft insects, caterpillars and little grubs. Lots of them.'

Nila thought about this. She watched me again. She saw me fly to the meter box and find it taped, and sit on the wire, and look at the smooth grey wall. Then she did something no one had done before. Instead of deciding what I needed, she watched to see what I was looking for.
'Amma,' she said, 'he isn't hungry. He wants a house.'

The next Sunday Nila and her mother made a box from old wooden planks left over from the building work. It had a sloping roof, so the rain ran off, and a round hole in the front about 3 centimetres wide. 'Any bigger and the mynas can get in,' said her mother, who had looked it up. They hung it high on the wall under the edge of the roof, out of the afternoon sun, where cats could not reach.
Then Nila went to her father and said, 'Please don't cut the weeds in the corner. The caterpillars live there.'
Her father looked at her for a long moment. 'It looks untidy,' he said.
'It's the sparrows' kitchen,' said Nila.
Her father laughed, and the weeds stayed.

I did not trust the box at first. It smelled of new wood and people. I sat on the wire for three days and looked at it. Then my wife went in, and came out, and went in again, and I knew. We carried in straw and threads, a pigeon's feather, and a bit of red wool that Nila left on the windowsill for us.

Now, in the dark of the box, four chicks are cheeping. All day I fly to the sparrows' kitchen in the corner and back. Caterpillar. Grub. Caterpillar. Little green fly. Nila sits on the step and counts my trips on her fingers. Yesterday she ran out of fingers and borrowed her father's.
I never ate her bread again. But I think she knows that I am grateful.
item.epiphany: Nila first gives Chirri what she imagines a sparrow needs (bread), and it doesn't help. The turn comes when she stops deciding and starts watching. She sees that Chirri needs shelter (a hole for a nest) and the right food for chicks (insects from the 'weeds'). The hidden idea is the habitat: every animal needs their own kind of food, water and shelter, and caring means finding out what another living thing really needs.
ask: Why didn't the bread help Chirri?
What did Chirri really need? How did Nila find out?
Why was the new concrete house a problem for sparrows?
Nila's father called the long grass 'weeds'. Nila called it 'the sparrows' kitchen'. Who was right?
What could you watch, near your home, to find out what an animal needs?

item.title: The Lorax
item.author: Dr. Seuss
item.why: 'Unless someone like you cares a whole awful lot, nothing is going to get better. It's not.' A funny, sad story about what happens when all the trees are cut.

lessons.title: Changes we can undo and changes we can't

flagged.item: mixing: some mixtures can be separated, some can't

item: two or more materials mixed together

item.title: Egg and toast
item.question: Can cooking be undone?
need: a ladle of dosa batter, or a slice of bread
a pan or tawa and a stove
steps: Crack the egg into a bowl. Look at the white: runny and see-through.
A grown-up cooks the egg in the pan. Watch the white change.
A grown-up cooks a dosa on the tawa, or toasts the bread. Compare it with raw batter or untoasted bread: colour, smell, feel, and the sound when you break it.
Try to turn either back.
item.predict: Ask: 'What will the egg white look like when it's cooked? Can we make it raw again?'
item.observe: The egg white turns from clear and runny to white and solid. The runny batter becomes a crisp, brown dosa that smells different.
item.why: Heat changes the materials in the egg and the batter into new materials. In egg white, long folded molecules called proteins unfold and tangle together, so the white sets solid and stops being see-through. On a dosa or toast, sugars and proteins on the surface react and make brown, tasty new substances. These are irreversible changes: cooling does not undo them.
item.safety: A grown-up handles the stove and hot pan. Children watch from a safe distance.

item.who: The phlogiston theory (Georg Ernst Stahl and others, early 1700s), and Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794) and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier (1758–1836), France
item.idea: Phlogiston theory said that things which burn contain a fire-stuff, phlogiston, which escapes into the air as they burn. Ash was what was left after the phlogiston had gone.
item.then: Most chemists accepted it for most of the 1700s. It explained many things. But some metals got heavier when heated in air, which was hard to explain if something was escaping.
item.now: Lavoisier weighed everything, including the air, and showed that burning is a material combining with part of the air, which he named oxygen. Marie-Anne worked beside him: she translated English chemistry papers for him, drew the detailed plates for his great book, and kept the laboratory records. Phlogiston theory was abandoned.
item.ask: Phlogiston was wrong, but it helped people ask good questions. What clue showed it was wrong? Why do you think Marie-Anne's name is less famous than Antoine's?

item.who: Michael Faraday (1791–1867), England
item.idea: Faraday gave Christmas lectures for young people at the Royal Institution in London called 'The Chemical History of a Candle' (given in 1848 and 1860, published as a book in 1861). He showed that a burning candle melts, draws liquid wax up its wick, turns it to gas and burns it, making water and carbon dioxide.
item.then: Faraday had almost no schooling: he was the son of a blacksmith and worked as a bookbinder's apprentice, reading the science books he bound. He became one of the greatest scientists of his age.
item.now: His explanation of the candle is still correct, and the lectures are still read and repeated. The Royal Institution Christmas Lectures continue today.
item.ask: Faraday learned science by reading the books he was binding. What do you need to become a scientist: a school, or something else?

lessons.title: Day and night: why the Sun seems to move across the sky

item.who: Carl Linnaeus (1707–1778), Sweden
item.idea: In 1751 he described a 'flower clock': a garden of flowers that open and close at different hours, so you could tell the time by which ones were open.
item.then: People loved the idea and tried planting such clocks.
item.now: Many flowers do open and close at regular times, partly because of light and partly because of their own inner clocks. But gardeners who planted flower clocks found they worked only roughly, because flowers change their times with weather, season and place.
item.ask: If a flower opens at 6 am in Sweden, would it open at 6 am in Chennai too? How could you find out?

item.title: Moonbear's Shadow
item.author: Frank Asch
item.why: A bear tries to get rid of his shadow, and finds that it changes with the time of day: funny, and good science.

item.title: Marble maze
need: a marble, or a dried chana
steps: Draw a start and a finish on the lid.
Glue straws or card strips as walls to make a twisting path.
Tilt the lid to roll the marble from start to finish.
Each time the marble hits a wall, say 'direction change!'
Make it harder with more turns.
item.outcome: A working maze, and a child who can explain that each wall pushes the marble a new way.

item.title: Design a catapult
steps: Make a spoon catapult: tie a plastic spoon to a block or a stack of ice-cream sticks with rubber bands.
Load a paper ball and press down the spoon. Let go.
Change one thing at a time: press further down, or use two rubber bands.
Measure how far the ball goes each time in steps.
Explain which part is bending and springing back, and why a bigger bend throws further.
item.outcome: A working catapult and a chart of what made it shoot further.

item.who: Alfred Sturtevant (1891–1970), USA, and the tongue-rolling rule
item.idea: In 1940 Sturtevant, a respected geneticist, reported that being able to roll your tongue into a tube seemed to be inherited by one simple gene, with 'roller' winning over 'non-roller'. It went into many schoolbooks as the classic example.
item.then: In the 1950s other scientists studied identical twins and found pairs where one twin could roll and the other couldn't, which a single simple gene can't explain. Some people also learned to do it.
item.now: Rejected as a simple one-gene rule. Tongue rolling may be partly influenced by genes but is not the simple example books claimed, yet you can still find it in textbooks.
item.ask: If identical twins have the same genes, what does it tell you when one can do something and the other can't?

lessons.title: How living things grow

item.who: Rita Levi-Montalcini (1909–2012), Italy and the USA
item.idea: When Mussolini's 1938 racial laws barred Jewish scientists from universities, Levi-Montalcini set up a laboratory in her bedroom and studied how nerves grow in chick embryos, using sewing needles as tools. Later, in the USA in the 1950s, she and Stanley Cohen discovered nerve growth factor (NGF), a chemical messenger that tells nerve cells to grow and where to go.
item.then: Many scientists doubted for years that a single chemical could guide growth like this; some thought her results were a mistake.
item.now: Accepted. She and Cohen shared the Nobel Prize in 1986, and many other growth factors, the body's 'grow here' messages, are now known. She kept working until she was over 100.
item.ask: She did important science in a bedroom, with sewing needles, when she was banned from universities. What do you think a scientist really needs?

lessons.title: Habitats: how plants and animals are suited to their homes

animal signs: tracks, droppings, nests, holes and nibbles

item: a very small habitat inside a bigger one, like the underside of a leaf or the inside of a log
water in the air turning back into drops on a cool surface

item.who: Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward (1791–1868), England
item.idea: Ward was a London doctor who could not grow ferns in his garden because of the city's smoke. Around 1829 he noticed a fern and some grass sprouting in a sealed glass bottle where he had put a moth chrysalis in damp soil. The plants lived inside for years without new water. He designed sealed glass cases, called Wardian cases, and showed that plants could survive long sea journeys inside them.
item.then: Plant collectors quickly took up the cases, and plants that used to die on ships now arrived alive. The cases carried tea from China to India, rubber from South America to Asia, and many other plants around the world. Often this made money for empires rather than for the people whose plants they were.
item.now: His discovery is accepted: a sealed case keeps its water going round and keeps its air moist. The bottle gardens people keep today come from his idea.
item.ask: Ward found his discovery by accident, because he noticed something odd in a bottle. What would you need to do to notice an accident like that?

item.who: Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859), Germany, and Aimé Bonpland (1773–1858), France
item.idea: In 1802, travelling in South America, Humboldt and the plant scientist Bonpland climbed high up the volcano Chimborazo with local guides. They noted that plants change in bands as you go up: hot forest at the bottom, then cooler forest, then grassland, then only mosses and lichens near the snow. Humboldt drew a famous picture showing which plants live at which height. He saw that climbing a mountain is like travelling towards the cold poles.
item.then: His books made him famous across Europe. Bonpland, who did much of the plant collecting and describing, became much less famous. The local guides and Indigenous people who knew the mountains were hardly named at all.
item.now: Scientists accept that plants and animals live in zones set by temperature and rain. Today they are watching many mountain plants move higher up as the climate warms.
item.ask: If plants are moving up mountains as the Earth warms, what happens to the plants that already live at the very top?

item.title: Island: A Story of the Galápagos
item.author: Jason Chin
item.why: An island rises from the sea, and plants and animals arrive and change to fit it. A first look at how living things become suited to a place.

lessons.title: Staying healthy: what keeps a growing body well

item.who: Willoughby D. Miller (1853–1907), an American dentist working in Berlin
item.idea: For thousands of years, people in Babylon, India, China and Europe believed that a 'tooth worm' made holes in teeth. In 1890 Miller published 'The Micro-organisms of the Human Mouth'. He showed that bacteria living on teeth turn sugars and starch into acid, and that the acid dissolves enamel.
item.then: His idea was built on Pasteur and Koch's new germ science and was widely taken up by dentists.
item.now: Scientists today agree that tooth decay is caused by acid from plaque bacteria feeding on sugar, with diet, saliva and fluoride all playing a part. Nobody has ever found a tooth worm.
item.ask: People believed in the tooth worm for thousands of years. Why do you think nobody checked? How could you check?

lessons.title: Comparing animals: fur, feathers, scales and legs
Light and dark: what makes light, and why we need it to see

item: the black circle in the middle of your eye that lets light in

item.title: Watch your pupils
item.question: How do our eyes change in dim and bright light?
need: a room you can make dim
steps: Make the room dim and wait one minute.
Sit facing each other and look at the black circle (the pupil) in each other's eyes.
Switch on the lamp, pointed away from your faces.
Watch the pupils straight away. What happens?
Switch it off and watch again.
item.predict: Ask: 'Will the black circle get bigger or smaller when the light comes on?'
item.observe: The pupils shrink quickly in bright light and slowly grow again in dim light.
item.why: The pupil is a hole that lets light into the eye. In dim light it opens wide to catch as much light as possible. In bright light it closes to protect the inside of the eye. It happens by itself, without you deciding.
item.safety: Never point the lamp into the eyes. Never use the Sun.

item.who: Sara Lewis (Tufts University, USA) and other firefly scientists (study published 2020)
item.idea: Fireflies flash to find each other. In 2020 Sara Lewis and colleagues asked firefly experts around the world what threatens fireflies most. They named habitat loss first, then light pollution (bright lights at night), then pesticides. Experiments show that bright light can stop some fireflies from flashing and finding mates.
item.then: Many people had noticed fewer fireflies than when they were children, but few scientists had measured it.
item.now: Scientists agree that light at night disturbs fireflies, turtle hatchlings, moths and birds. How much each threat matters, and how many firefly kinds are actually disappearing, is still debated, because good long counts are rare, especially in India.
item.ask: Your grandparents may say there were more fireflies when they were young. Is that good evidence? How could you count fireflies to find out for sure?

lessons.title: Natural, made and tested: choosing materials like a scientist

flagged.item: a testable question

item: a chart of blocks or bars that shows numbers so you can compare them
two overlapping circles for sorting things that can belong to both groups
it can be broken down by tiny living things, such as bacteria and fungi, into soil, water and gases

item.title: The burial test
item.question: Which materials can the soil break down?
need: a large pot or tub of damp soil, from a potted plant or a nursery bag
small pieces of banana peel, cotton rag, newspaper, plastic bag, foil and a leaf
steps: Bury each piece about 5 cm deep in a different part of the pot.
Mark each with a labelled lolly stick.
Keep the soil damp, not soaking, in a shady place.
On Day 5, check only the banana peel.
On Day 8, dig everything up and compare. If you can, wait until two weeks have passed since you buried them.
item.predict: Write your child's prediction for each piece: gone, changed, or the same.
item.observe: The banana peel and leaf turn brown, soft and broken. The newspaper and cotton go soft and may start to fall apart. The plastic and foil look almost the same.
item.why: Bacteria, fungi and small animals like worms feed on materials made from living things: peel, leaves, paper and cotton. These are biodegradable. Most plastics are made of long chains that these living things cannot easily break down, so they stay for a very long time and only break into smaller pieces. Foil is a metal and does not rot.
item.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Use soil from a plant pot or a nursery, not from a drain or a dump.

item.title: The great audition
steps: The grown-up is the director.
The child plays each material trying out for a job, boasting about a property and admitting a weakness.
The director asks a hard question.
The child chooses the winner and gives a reason.
Change the job and see if the winner changes.
item.outcome: Your child sees that 'best' depends on the job, and can argue from properties.

item.title: Rosie Revere, Engineer
item.author: Andrea Beaty

lessons.title: Order, mess and chance: what we can and can't predict

item: tiny pieces of something spreading out by themselves, from where there are many to where there are few, like a smell crossing a room
the scientists' word for how mixed and spread out things are. Left alone, entropy goes up.

item.title: Kolam and splatter
need: an old toothbrush or a spoon
steps: Rule art: draw a 3 by 3 grid of dots.
Draw one line that curves around every dot, never touches a dot, and comes back to where it began.
Chance art: cover the floor with newspaper.
Dip the toothbrush in paint and flick the bristles with a finger over the second sheet, or drip paint from a spoon.
Put the two pictures side by side.
item.outcome: Two pictures: one made by a rule that could be made again, and one made by chance that can never be made exactly again.

item.who: Ludwig Boltzmann (1844–1906), Austria
item.idea: He explained heat and mixing using the idea that everything is made of tiny atoms moving at random. He showed that things spread out because there are far more ways for atoms to be spread out than bunched up. His way of counting ways is the root of the idea scientists call entropy.
item.then: Many leading scientists of his time, such as Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, did not believe atoms were real, and argued hard against him. He was often unhappy about being doubted, and died in 1906.
item.now: Within a few years of his death, experiments on tiny jiggling particles in water (explained by Albert Einstein in 1905 and tested by Jean Perrin) convinced nearly everyone that atoms are real. His counting idea is now a basic part of physics and chemistry.
item.ask: Boltzmann was right but many people did not believe him. What kind of evidence would have convinced you that atoms are real?

item.who: Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), Italy
item.idea: A doctor and mathematician who also loved playing dice games. He wrote a book about games of chance, one of the first to count the ways dice can fall. He saw that with a fair die each face is equally likely.
item.then: His book on chance was only printed in 1663, long after he died. By then Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat had worked out probability in their letters of 1654, and they usually get the credit for starting it.
item.now: Historians agree that Cardano had many of the key ideas first, even though few people read them in his lifetime. Probability is now used everywhere, from weather forecasts to medicine.
item.ask: Cardano wrote his ideas first, but Pascal and Fermat usually get the credit. Who do you think should be remembered, and why? Does it matter when a book gets printed?

item.title: Probably Pistachio
item.author: Stuart J. Murphy
item.why: A boy guesses what will happen on a bad day, and learns the language of probably and probably not.

lessons.title: Our closest cousins: the apes and monkeys who are family to us

item.title: Through the Treetops
need: a coin or button for each player
rules: Each player puts a coin on START.
Take turns to roll the die and move that many squares.
Read the square aloud. Do what it says. If it asks a question, answer it first. A grown-up checks the answer.
If the answer is wrong, stay where you are this turn.
The first player to reach HOME, the nest at the top of the tallest tree, wins.
At the end, each player says one thing they learned from a square.
squares: START: the forest floor
A fig tree is full of ripe fruit. Move ahead 2.
Question: does an ape have a tail? (No.)
The next tree is too far. Sway your tree like an orangutan. Move ahead 1.
You did not look with both eyes and missed a branch. Go back 2.
Question: name one ape who lives in Africa. (Chimpanzee, bonobo or gorilla.)
A termite mound! Strip a twig to make a tool. Move ahead 2.
Grip a branch with your feet like a chimpanzee. Move ahead 1.
Question: what is India's only ape? (The hoolock gibbon.)
A friend grooms your fur. Rest here and miss nothing.
Question: who watched chimpanzees in Tanzania from 1960? (Jane Goodall.)
A storm comes. Hold a big leaf over your head. Move ahead 1.
The trees here were cut down. Go back 3.
Question: what do primates have on their fingers instead of claws? (Nails.)
A silverback beats his chest. Stay still and miss a turn.
Question: are humans the grandchildren of chimpanzees, or their cousins? (Cousins.)
Bonobo friends share their fruit with you. Move ahead 2.
Question: what does an orangutan build almost every night? (A nest.)
You see your face in a pool of water and know it is you. Move ahead 1.
Question: why do primates have eyes at the front? (To judge how far away a branch is.)
Gibbons sing their morning duet. Sing it too, then move ahead 1.
Question: why are many apes in danger? (Their forests are being cut down.)
HOME: the nest at the top of the tallest tree

item.who: Sarah Brosnan, USA, and Frans de Waal (1948–2024), Netherlands and USA, scientists who study primates
item.idea: In 2003 Brosnan and de Waal trained capuchin monkeys to hand back a small stone in return for food. When one monkey got a grape and her neighbour got cucumber for the same job, the neighbour often refused the cucumber or threw it away. De Waal also spent many years watching chimpanzees hug and kiss to make up after fights.
item.then: The test became famous, because it seemed to show that monkeys notice when something is unfair.
item.now: Scientists still argue. Some say the monkeys really react to unfairness. Others say they may just be upset that a better food was there and they did not get it. Similar reactions have been seen in chimpanzees and dogs.
item.ask: How could you test whether the monkey is upset about her neighbour, or only about the grape?

lessons.title: Rocks and soil: what the ground under us is made of

flagged.item: rocks that absorb water and rocks that are waterproof

item: to soak up water, the way chalk or a sponge does
does not let water soak in, like slate or a polished granite floor
the dark part of soil made from dead leaves and animals that have rotted

item.who: Graham Cairns-Smith (1931–2016), chemist, Glasgow, Scotland
item.idea: In the 1960s and later, in his book 'Seven Clues to the Origin of Life' (1985), Cairns-Smith suggested that the first steps towards life might have used clay. Clay is made of tiny crystals, and crystals grow and copy their pattern. He thought clay crystals could have held a pattern before living things had genes.
item.then: Most scientists were looking for the start of life only in special chemicals in water.
item.now: Minority. Few scientists think clay crystals were the first 'life'. But many agree that rock and clay surfaces may have helped the first chemicals of life join up. Nobody knows yet how life began.
item.ask: Nobody saw life begin. How could scientists ever test an idea like this?

item.title: The dry tissue
item.question: Is an 'empty' tumbler really empty?
need: a bucket or big vessel of water, deeper than the tumbler
steps: Push the tissue into the bottom of the tumbler so it stays stuck when you turn the tumbler over.
Turn the tumbler upside down.
Push it straight down into the water, all the way under. Keep it straight.
Hold it there for 5 seconds.
Lift it straight up and out. Feel the tissue.
Now push it in again and tip it a little. Watch the bubble.
item.predict: Ask: 'Will the tissue get wet? Why do you think so?'
item.observe: The tissue stays dry when the tumbler goes in straight. When you tip it, a bubble of air escapes and water rushes in.
item.why: The tumbler was full of air. Air is made of matter, like water and stone, so it takes up space. While the air was trapped, the water could not fill that space, so it stopped near the mouth of the tumbler and the tissue stayed dry. When the tumbler tipped, the air escaped as a bubble and the water took its place.
item.safety: Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.

item.title: Fold a wormhole
steps: Draw a dot near the top and one near the bottom of the paper.
Draw a straight line between them.
Fold the paper so the two dots touch.
Push the pencil through both dots.
item.outcome: A paper model of the wormhole idea, and the knowledge that it is an idea from maths that nobody has found in nature.

item.title: The sticker test
item.question: Who knows that the face in the mirror is their own?
need: a small bindi or skin-safe sticker
a toddler visitor (only with their parent's permission)
steps: Earlier in the day, during a hug or tickle, put a bindi or sticker on your child's forehead without saying anything.
Later, hand them a mirror and watch: do they reach up and touch their own forehead?
Hold the mirror in front of a pet, if you have one. Do they look behind the mirror, bark, ignore it or touch themselves?
If a toddler is visiting and their parent agrees, try the bindi and mirror with them too.
Write down what each one did.
item.predict: Ask: 'Will a cat know that the cat in the mirror is herself? Will a baby?'
item.observe: Your child touches their own forehead. Pets usually ignore the mirror or treat the reflection as another animal. Children from about 18 months to 2 years old usually touch the mark. Younger babies often treat the mirror baby as a playmate.
item.why: Touching the mark on your own face, after seeing it in a mirror, shows you understand the reflection is you. This is the mirror test, invented by Gordon Gallup in 1970. Chimpanzees, Asian elephants and magpies have passed versions of it. But animals that live by smell or sound, like dogs, may know themselves in other ways, so a mirror may be an unfair test for them.
item.safety: Use a skin-safe sticker. Never force an animal to look in a mirror. Stop if they seem upset.

item.title: Camouflage hunt
need: a sheet of coloured paper (red, yellow or blue)
steps: Tear 15 small bits, each about the size of a fingernail, from one newspaper sheet, and 15 bits the same size from the coloured paper.
Spread the other two newspaper sheets flat on the floor. While your child looks away, scatter all 30 bits over them.
Your child is a hungry bird. They have 30 seconds to pick up as many 'caterpillars' as they can, one at a time.
Count how many of each kind they found. Then do it again for another 30 seconds, and count again.
Look together for the ones still hidden.
item.outcome: A count showing that the coloured bits are found first and the newspaper bits hide best. This is how camouflage protects animals.

item.who: Gordon Gallup (born 1941), USA, and Masanori Kohda and colleagues (2019), Japan
item.idea: In 1970 Gallup put a coloured mark on chimpanzees' faces while they were asleep under anaesthetic. When they woke and looked in a mirror, they touched the mark on their own faces. This 'mirror test' became a way to ask whether an animal knows itself. In 2019 Kohda's team reported that small cleaner fish (cleaner wrasse) with a mark on their throat tried to scrape it off after seeing themselves in a mirror.
item.then: Gallup and others doubted the fish result. They said the scraping might mean something else, and that a test designed for apes may not tell us about fish.
item.now: Great apes, Asian elephants (an elephant called Happy, in 2006) and Eurasian magpies have passed versions of the test. Dogs usually fail it, yet experiments suggest dogs know their own smell. Whether the mirror test really measures knowing yourself, and whether the fish passed, is still argued.
item.ask: A dog fails the mirror test but can tell their own smell from other dogs' smells. Does the dog know themself? Is a mirror a fair test for a dog?

item.title: The Landing Lights
text: I am a worker bee from the hive in the hollow of the old drumstick tree behind Building C. I am twenty-one days old, which, for a bee, is old enough to be trusted with the sky.

Every morning, when the sun clears the water tank, I fly the same road: over the wall, past the washing lines, up to the fourth-floor balcony where the girl keeps her pots. There are marigolds there, and tulsi, and a hibiscus, and one tall sunflower that leans over the railing as if it is trying to see the street.

The girl is called Malar. I know because her mother calls it out of the kitchen window twenty times a day. Malar is seven. She is a great deal bigger than me and a great deal slower, and she smells of soap and mango and the sticky chalk she draws with.
She has been watching me.

Yesterday she sat on a stool beside the sunflower with a notebook on her knees. She was painting it. I came in as I always do, straight to the middle of the flower, and walked down the dark road to where the nectar is. She leaned so close that her breath ruffled my wings.
“Amma,” she called. “Why do the bees always land in the same place? Right in the middle. Every time. As if somebody drew a circle for them.”

Somebody did draw a circle, I wanted to tell her. Can't you see it? The sunflower's petals are not one colour. Near the tips they glow, and near the middle they go dark, darker, darkest, in a great ring, like the lights on a runway at night, all pointing in. Any bee can see it.
But Malar's painting had petals of one plain yellow, from tip to tip. She had not drawn the ring at all.

I thought she must be careless. Then I thought she must be strange. Then I flew home with my nectar and forgot her, because my sisters were dancing in the warm dark of the hive. A bee's dance tells the others which way to fly and how far. Today's dance said: flowers, towards the morning sun, not far.
Today she was waiting for me with a book.

Her mother sat beside her, still in her office clothes, glasses pushed up into her hair. The book was open at two pictures of the same flower. In the first, the flower was plain yellow, like Malar's painting. In the second, the petals had gone pale at the tips and dark in the middle: a great ring, pointing in.
“This one is taken with an ordinary camera,” said her mother. “And this one with a special camera that can see a kind of light called ultraviolet. Our eyes can't see it. Bees can.”
Malar looked at the second picture for a long time. Then she looked at the sunflower. Then she looked at me.
“So it's there,” she said slowly. “The circle is really there. Right now. I just can't see it.”
“It's there for the bee,” said her mother.
“But is it real?”
Her mother smiled. “What do you think?”
Malar frowned the frown I have seen on bees deciding whether a flower is worth the trip. “It must be real,” she said. “Because the bee lands on it. Every time. If it wasn't real, she'd miss.”
I did not miss. I landed, I walked the dark road, I drank.
Then Malar asked a question that no human has asked in all my twenty-one days. It was a question about me that was really a question about herself.
“Amma, if there's a colour I can't see, are there colours I can see that the bee can't?”
Her mother turned towards the hibiscus. “Red,” she said. “Honeybees can't see red the way we do. To a bee, that hibiscus probably looks dark. Almost like a shadow.”
Malar stared at the hibiscus. It is the flower she loves best. I have heard her tell it so. To me it has always been a dull, quiet thing, a dark cup that only the sunbirds bother with.
“But it's the brightest thing on the balcony,” she whispered. “It's practically shouting.”
“For you,” said her mother.

Malar was quiet for a while. A crow went past. Somebody downstairs was frying mustard seeds, and the smell came up the building in a warm cloud that I could have followed with my eyes shut. Then Malar tore yesterday's page out of her notebook and began again.

This time she painted the petals pale at the tips and dark at the base, and in the middle a ring, dark as she could make it, pointing in. Next to it she painted the hibiscus, but grey, the colour of a shadow. Underneath she wrote big crooked letters, which I cannot read. Her mother read them aloud: “The balcony, for a bee.”

When she propped the painting against the pot and went inside for lunch, I did something foolish. I flew to the painting. I landed right in the middle of her dark ring and walked the road inwards, and of course there was no nectar at all, only paper and the bitter smell of paint.
I stayed anyway, longer than a sensible bee should. The sun was warm on my back. Somewhere inside, Malar was laughing at something her mother had said.
She is trying to see my world, I thought. She will never quite manage it. And I have never once seen her red, the shouting red, and I never will.

I flew home with no nectar and danced no dance. I stood for a long time in the warm dark among my sisters, thinking about the girl and the grey hibiscus, and about all the things that might be shining, right now, right in front of both of us, that neither of us can see.
item.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Malar realises the ring is 'really there' because the bee never misses. Then she turns the question round: are there colours she sees that the bee can't? The idea in the story is that what is real is bigger than what any one being senses. Bees see ultraviolet but not red, and people see red but not ultraviolet, so nobody sees 'the whole flower'. The bee's last thought keeps the question open.
ask: What did the bee see on the sunflower that Malar couldn't?
How did Malar work out that the ring was real, even though she couldn't see it?
What did the hibiscus look like to the bee? Why was Malar surprised?
Why do you think the bee landed on the painting, even though there was no nectar?
Who sees the real flower: Malar, the bee, or neither?

item.who: Vibhu Prakash and the scientists who solved India's vulture crash (1990s–2000s)
item.idea: In the 1990s Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society noticed that vultures in Keoladeo National Park, Bharatpur, were dying. Surveys showed that India's white-rumped vultures, once among the commonest big birds in the world, fell by more than 95% in about 15 years. In 2004 a team led by Lindsay Oaks, working in Pakistan, found the cause: diclofenac, a painkiller given to sick cattle. Vultures that ate the carcasses of treated cattle died of kidney failure.
item.then: At first some people blamed a disease. Finding the real cause took years of careful testing of dead birds.
item.now: Accepted. India banned diclofenac for animals in 2006. Breeding centres such as the one at Pinjore in Haryana are raising vultures to release, but numbers are still a tiny part of what they were, and other harmful animal painkillers are still being found.
item.ask: The medicine was meant to help cows. How could the people who made it have found out it might harm vultures? Whose job should it be to check?

item.who: The wolves of Yellowstone: William Ripple and Robert Beschta, and their critics (USA, 1995 onwards)
item.idea: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995–96, about 70 years after they had been killed off there. Ripple and Beschta argued that the wolves made the elk move around more and graze less by the rivers, so willows and aspen trees grew back, beavers returned, and even the riverbanks changed shape. This chain of effects is called a trophic cascade.
item.then: The story became hugely popular, with videos saying 'wolves changed rivers'.
item.now: Debated. Other scientists, such as Arthur Middleton and Matthew Kauffman, found that elk were not as scared of wolves as claimed, and that hunting by people, bears and cougars, dry years, and the loss of beavers mattered too. Most agree the wolves had some effect; how big it was is still argued.
item.ask: Why do people love a story where one hero animal fixes everything? What evidence would you need to be sure it was the wolves?

lessons.title: Family: kinds of family, relatives and sharing the work

item: the oldest female who leads a family, like a grandmother elephant

item.title: Relation Rummy
rules: Cut out the cards. Each set has three cards: the relation, its word in one language, and its word in another.
Shuffle and deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the pile.
On your turn, take a card from the pile, then throw one away face up.
When you have a set of three that match (the same relation), lay it down and say the relation aloud.
The first player to lay down two sets wins. Then everyone says what they call that relative at home.

item.who: Douglas Rohde, Steve Olson and Joseph Chang, USA (published in Nature, 2004)
item.idea: Using computer models of how people have moved and had children over thousands of years, they estimated that the most recent person who is an ancestor of every human alive today may have lived only a few thousand years ago. A few thousand years further back, every person alive was either an ancestor of everyone living now, or of no one.
item.then: Many people were surprised, because we usually think of family trees as separate. Others pointed out that islands and isolated groups could push the dates further back.
item.now: The mathematics is accepted: family trees must join, and all humans share recent common ancestors. The exact dates are uncertain and depend on how much people moved and mixed, so they are still debated.
item.ask: If every person alive shares ancestors who lived only a few thousand years ago, what does that mean for the way people divide themselves into 'us' and 'them'?

item.who: Cynthia Moss (born 1940), USA, working in Amboseli, Kenya
item.idea: Since 1972 Moss and her team in the Amboseli Elephant Research Project have followed the same elephant families, generation after generation. They found that elephant families are led by the oldest female, the matriarch, and that calves are cared for by many females. With Karen McComb and others, they showed in 2001 that families led by older matriarchs are better at telling the calls of friendly families from the calls of strangers. Later work showed that older matriarchs also judge the danger from lions better, because they have learned more in their long lives.
item.then: Early elephant studies paid most attention to big males and their tusks. Moss's patient, decades-long watching of females and families changed the picture.
item.now: It is accepted: elephant families are matriarchal, and old females carry knowledge that helps everyone survive. Elephants with old matriarchs killed by poachers can lose that knowledge.
item.ask: Why might an elephant family need its oldest member most of all? Who carries that kind of knowledge in a human family?

item.who: Marilyn Waring (born 1952), New Zealand
item.idea: In her book If Women Counted (1988), Waring showed that the way countries measure their economy leaves out unpaid work done at home, such as cooking, cleaning, caring for children and elders, and fetching water, most of which is done by women. So the work that keeps families alive appears to be worth nothing.
item.then: Many economists said this kind of work was too hard to measure. Waring's work helped persuade countries to run time-use surveys, which measure how people spend their day.
item.now: It is accepted that unpaid care work is huge and mostly done by women; India's first national Time Use Survey (2019) found women spending about five hours a day on it and men about one and a half. How it should be counted and valued is still debated.
item.ask: If cooking at home were paid like cooking in a restaurant, would people value it more? Is everything valuable something that should have a price?

item.who: Coluthur Gopalan (1918–2019), India
item.idea: Gopalan led the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad. With his colleagues he measured the nutrients in hundreds of Indian foods, published in the book 'Nutritive Value of Indian Foods'. In the 1960s, many experts from rich countries said that hungry children in poor countries mainly lacked protein, and planned special protein foods. Gopalan and others studied what Indian children really ate. They found that most undernourished children were not getting enough food overall. With enough of the usual rice or roti with dal, most would get enough protein too.
item.then: International bodies spent years and money on special protein foods. Some experts resisted the idea that the real gap was simply not enough food.
item.now: By the 1970s most nutrition scientists agreed that the 'protein gap' had been overstated, and that most hungry children needed more food overall. Gopalan's food tables are still used in India today.
item.ask: Experts far away guessed what Indian children needed. Gopalan measured it. Why is measuring better than guessing, and who should be asked?

lessons.title: Gravity: every object attracts every other object

item.who: Robert Hooke (1635–1703) and Isaac Newton (1643–1727), England
item.idea: In letters to Newton in 1679–1680, Hooke suggested that the planets move as they do because of a pull towards the Sun that weakens with the square of the distance (twice as far, a quarter of the pull). Newton worked out the mathematics and published the law of universal gravitation in his Principia in 1687.
item.then: Hooke felt Newton had taken his idea without credit and said so. Newton was furious and removed some mentions of Hooke from his book. Newton later became president of the Royal Society, after Hooke died.
item.now: Historians agree Hooke suggested the inverse-square idea and that Newton did the mathematical proof that made it a law; they still argue over how much credit each deserves. Newton was brilliant, and he also fought hard over credit with Hooke, Flamsteed and Leibniz. Hooke, poor-born and endlessly inventive, is far less remembered.
item.ask: If one person has an idea and another proves it, who discovered it? Should a law be named after one person or two?

item.who: Jane Goodall (1934–2025), England
item.idea: In 1960 Jane Goodall, a young woman with no university degree, began watching chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania. After months of patient sitting, she saw a chimpanzee she named David Greybeard strip leaves off a stem and use it to fish termites out of a mound. She showed that chimpanzees make and use tools, hunt, and have strong family bonds and their own personalities.
item.then: Many scientists said only humans made tools. Some criticised her for naming the chimpanzees instead of numbering them, and for describing their feelings. Her mentor, Louis Leakey, said the finding meant people would have to rethink what makes humans special.
item.now: Her findings are accepted. Many animals, including crows, elephants and octopuses, are now known to use tools. Studying animals as individuals with feelings is normal science.
item.ask: Why do you think it took a person who sat quietly for months, rather than someone who visited for a day, to see the chimpanzees use tools?

item.who: Bernie Krause (born 1938), USA
item.idea: Krause, a musician, spent decades recording the sounds of wild places around the world. He noticed that in healthy, undisturbed places the animals seemed to call at separate pitches and separate times, like instruments in an orchestra, so each could be heard. In the 1990s he called this the 'acoustic niche' idea. He named the sounds made by living things 'biophony'.
item.then: Some ecologists liked the idea and began using sound recordings to check the health of forests and reefs. Others found places where many animals call at the same pitches and times, so the orchestra pattern is not always there.
item.now: Listening to habitats, called soundscape ecology, is now a real tool for scientists. Whether animals truly share out the sound the way Krause suggested is still argued. It seems to happen in some places and not others.
item.ask: If you recorded your street at dawn now and again in ten years, what might the difference tell you?
