lessons.title: How life began on Earth

flagged.item: creation stories from many cultures, respected alongside the science

item.who: Mary Anning (1799–1847), Lyme Regis, England
item.idea: From childhood Anning hunted fossils in the crumbling cliffs to sell to visitors and support her poor family. Around 1811–12, with her brother Joseph, she found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised by scientists, and in 1823 a nearly complete plesiosaur. Her finds were strong evidence that strange creatures had lived long ago and vanished: extinction was real and the Earth very old.
item.then: As a working-class woman she could not join the Geological Society, and the gentlemen who bought her fossils often published them without naming her.
item.now: Accepted as one of the great fossil hunters. Her finds helped build the idea of deep time, and she is now honoured, with a statue in Lyme Regis since 2022.
item.ask: Anning found the fossils, but others wrote the papers. Who should get the credit for a discovery: the finder, the explainer, or both?

item.who: James Hutton (1726–1797), Scotland
item.idea: Hutton, a farmer and doctor, watched soil wash away and rocks slowly form. In 1788 at Siccar Point he showed his friends upright rock layers with flat layers on top, and explained that this needed unimaginable time: layers laid down, tilted, worn away, and new layers laid on top. He wrote that he could find 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end'.
item.then: Many people then believed the Earth was only a few thousand years old, and his ideas were attacked. His friend John Playfair later explained them in clearer words.
item.now: Deep time is accepted. Hutton was wrong that there was no beginning: in 1956 Clair Patterson measured the Earth's age at about 4.5 billion years using meteorites.
item.ask: Hutton saw deep time in a cliff. What everyday thing around you shows slow change, if you could only wait long enough?

item.title: Starlight barcode
need: sunlight or a bright tube light
steps: Hold the shiny side of the CD in light and tilt it until a band of rainbow colours appears.
Try to catch the band on white paper.
Name the colours in order.
Draw the spectrum on paper as a long strip.
Add a few thin black lines across it, like a barcode, and say: 'each kind of atom makes its own lines'.
item.outcome: A drawn spectrum and the idea that the colours in light show what made the light.

item.who: Marie Tharp (1920–2006), USA
item.idea: Working with Bruce Heezen at Columbia University from the early 1950s, Tharp turned thousands of ships' echo-depth readings into maps of the ocean floor. In 1952–53 she found a deep rift valley running down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a sign that the sea floor was splitting apart.
item.then: Heezen at first dismissed it as 'girl talk', she later said, because it seemed to support Wegener's moving continents, which most geologists still rejected. Women were not allowed on the research ships, so she worked only from the data the men collected. She first went to sea in 1968.
item.now: The rift turned out to run through all the oceans, matching lines of earthquakes. Along with other evidence, it helped prove plate tectonics in the 1960s. Her world ocean floor map, painted with Heinrich Berann and published in 1977, is famous.
item.ask: Tharp was not allowed on the ships for 16 years, yet she saw what the men on board missed. How could someone working only from the numbers see more clearly?

item.who: Martin Fleischmann (1927–2012) and Stanley Pons (born 1943), England and USA
item.idea: In March 1989, at a press conference at the University of Utah, they announced 'cold fusion': nuclear fusion, the energy of the Sun, happening in a jar of heavy water at room temperature, which would have meant almost endless cheap energy.
item.then: The news went round the world. Hundreds of labs rushed to repeat it. A few reported extra heat, but most found nothing, and the particles that fusion must produce were missing. Within months most scientists concluded the result was a mistake.
item.now: Cold fusion as claimed is rejected. A small number of researchers still study related effects, without convincing results so far. It is remembered as a warning: announce to the press before peer review, and with an extraordinary claim, and you need extraordinary evidence.
item.ask: Fleischmann and Pons were respected scientists who believed what they saw. What should they have done before telling the world?

item.title: Minibeast key
need: pictures or drawings of: ant, beetle, spider, woodlouse, earthworm, snail, butterfly, centipede
steps: Use this key first. 1: Does it have legs? No: go to 2. Yes: go to 3. 2: Does it have a shell? Yes: snail. No: earthworm. 3: Does it have more than 8 legs? Yes: go to 4. No: go to 5. 4: Does it have more than 20 legs? Yes: centipede. No: woodlouse. 5: Does it have 8 legs? Yes: spider. No: go to 6. 6: Does it have large coloured wings? Yes: butterfly. No: go to 7. 7: Does it have hard wing cases? Yes: beetle. No: ant.
Name each picture using the key.
Now your child makes their own key, with different questions, for four minibeasts from home: for example an ant, a cockroach, a housefly and a spider.

item.outcome: A key your child has used, and one they have made and tested.

item.who: Itty Achuden, a Kerala healer, and the Hortus Malabaricus (Amsterdam, 1678–1693)
item.idea: The Hortus Malabaricus ('Garden of Malabar') is a 12-volume book describing about 740 plants of the Kerala coast, with large engravings. It was made under the Dutch governor of Malabar, Hendrik van Rheede. Much of its knowledge came from Itty Achuden, an Ezhava physician from a family of traditional healers, who described the plants and their uses from his family's palm-leaf manuscripts, and from three Konkani scholars, Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit and Appu Bhat.
item.then: The book carries van Rheede's name. Itty Achuden's contribution appears in a signed certificate in Malayalam in the first volume: one of the first times Malayalam was printed in a European book. The plants were given Malayalam names alongside Latin ones.
item.now: Historians agree the book could not have been made without Kerala's healers and scholars. Linnaeus used it when he named plants, so some scientific names today trace back to Itty Achuden's knowledge.
item.ask: Itty Achuden knew the plants. The governor paid for the book. The artists drew the pictures. Whose name should be on the cover? Why?

lessons.title: The seven signs of life, and the tricky cases

item.who: Didier Raoult and colleagues (2003), France, and their critics
item.idea: They described the mimivirus, a 'giant virus' so big it was first mistaken for a bacterium, with far more genes than any virus known, including genes for jobs viruses aren't supposed to do. Some of them argued that giant viruses deserve their own branch on the tree of life.
item.then: Many virologists disagreed: giant or not, these viruses still can't copy themselves without a host cell.
item.now: There's no agreement. Some scientists say viruses are alive only inside a cell. Others say they are not alive at all. Others say the question itself is the wrong one.
item.ask: Should the word 'alive' have a sharp edge, or can some things be 'partly alive'?

lessons.title: Living in harmony: how living things share a home

item.who: Lucy King, Kenya and UK (beehive fence research, from 2007)
item.idea: Elephants raiding farms is a serious problem in Africa and in India. Lucy King and her colleagues in Kenya noticed that elephants avoid trees with beehives, because bees can sting them around the eyes and inside the trunk. In 2007 they showed that elephants walked away from the recorded sound of angry bees. They then tested fences made of beehives hung on a wire around farms. When an elephant pushes the wire, the hives swing and the bees come out.
item.then: The idea seemed strange at first. But early trials in Kenya found far fewer elephant raids on farms with beehive fences, and the farmers could also sell the honey.
item.now: Beehive fences have been tried in many countries in Africa and Asia, including some places in India. They work well in many trials, but not everywhere. In a drought the bees can leave, the fences need care, and very hungry elephants sometimes break through. Scientists are still studying where they work best.
item.ask: A village puts up beehive fences and has fewer elephant raids that year. Can we be sure the fences did it? What else might have changed?

item.who: Divya Mudappa and T. R. Shankar Raman, Nature Conservation Foundation, Valparai, Tamil Nadu, India
item.idea: Valparai is a town in the Anamalai hills, among tea and coffee gardens, next to rainforest. Since the early 2000s, ecologists Divya Mudappa and T. R. Shankar Raman have worked with tea companies and local people to replant native rainforest trees in damaged patches of forest. They also help wild animals, such as the endangered lion-tailed macaque, live alongside people, for example by helping them cross busy roads more safely.
item.then: Many people thought that once a forest was broken up by plantations and roads, its rare animals would disappear, and the small patches were not worth saving.
item.now: Their long studies show that even small, cared-for forest patches among plantations can keep many rare birds and animals alive, and the replanted patches are growing back. How well people and wildlife can share such crowded hills, with elephants and leopards there too, is still a hard question.
item.ask: Can a town and a rainforest share the same hills? What would you need to count, year after year, to know whether the lion-tailed macaques are doing well?

item.title: The kabadiwala's tray
need: steel clips and safety pins, small bits of paper, plastic bottle caps, foil balls, rubber bands and a spoon of rice
steps: Mix everything in the tray. This is a heap of rubbish.
Your child moves the magnet just above the heap and lifts out the magnetic pieces into one bowl.
Ask what is left, and how it could be sorted without a magnet.
Talk about how scrap yards and kabadiwalas sort metal.
item.outcome: A sorted heap, and a child who can say how a magnet separates iron and steel from everything else.

item.title: The Key in the Drain
text: Every Saturday morning, Salim anna pushes his cart down our lane in Madurai. 'Old paper! Old iron! Old paper, old iron!' he calls. His cart is piled high with newspapers, bottles and bent pots. In his shirt pocket he keeps a round black magnet on a string.

That Saturday, Amma sold him the lid of our old pressure cooker and a dented lota. Salim anna held his magnet against the lid. Click. It stuck so hard he had to twist it off. 'Steel,' he said, and threw the lid onto his pile of iron things.

Then he held the magnet against the lota. It did not stick. It just slid down the side and swung on its string. Salim anna smiled. 'Brass,' he said. 'Brass pays better than iron.' He put the lota in a separate sack.
'But brass is a metal too,' I said. 'Why didn't it stick?'
Salim anna laughed. 'Ask your science teacher, Meena. I only know that it works.' He gave me a toffee and pushed his cart on down the lane.
I forgot about it until the evening.

Appa came home late from the office. Amma had gone to my aunt's house in Dindigul for the night, so it was only Appa, me and my little brother Kannan, who was six and very hungry. Appa stood at our gate and took the house keys out of his pocket. A motorbike roared past. Appa jumped, and the keys slipped out of his fingers.
They fell onto the iron grating that covers the drain beside our gate. For one second they sat there. Then they slid through a gap and dropped with a soft plop into the dark water below.

Appa knelt down and shone his phone torch through the grating. The drain was about as deep as my arm, with muddy water at the bottom. We could see the keys lying in the mud: two yellow keys and the small silver ring that held them together. The grating was far too heavy to lift. The gaps between its bars were only as wide as two of my fingers.

'I can't get my hand in,' Appa said. 'We'll have to call a locksmith. He'll break the lock.' He looked at our front door. It was a good brass lock, and a new one would cost a lot. Kannan started to cry.
Then I thought of the magnet on a string.

I ran down the lane to the shed where Salim anna keeps his cart. He was eating his dinner on the step. When I told him, he put down his plate, took the magnet out of his pocket and walked back with me. He tied two more lengths of string to it, so it could reach the bottom.
Appa held the torch. Salim anna lowered the magnet between the bars. It swung once, and then, clack! It jumped sideways and stuck to a bar of the grating.

'The grating is iron,' said Salim anna. He pulled the magnet off and tried again. 'Down the middle of the gap. Slowly. Don't let it swing.' This time it went straight down, past the bars, and into the water.
We watched it reach the bottom. Salim anna moved it until it touched the keys. Then he pulled the string up slowly. The magnet came up out of the water, dripping. Nothing was stuck to it.
He tried again. And again. Each time the magnet came up with only mud on it.
'It's the water,' Appa said quietly. 'The water must be stopping the magnet.'
I looked down at the two yellow keys in the torchlight. Yellow, like Amma's lota. I thought about the lota sliding off the magnet that morning, and about the lid that stuck so hard.
'The keys are brass,' I said. 'Like the lota.'
Everyone looked at me. Salim anna's eyebrows went up.
'But the ring isn't,' I said. 'The ring is silver-coloured, like the cooker lid.'
Salim anna handed me the string. 'Then you do it,' he said.

My hands were shaking. I let the magnet down through the middle of the gap, slowly, so it did not swing. It went into the water. Appa moved the torch so I could see the small silver ring. I lowered the magnet until it was just above the ring, and then a tiny bit lower.
I felt it through the string: a small tug, like a fish nibbling.
I pulled up very, very slowly. Out of the water came the magnet. Hanging from it was the silver ring, and hanging from the ring, swinging and dripping, were our two yellow keys.

Kannan stopped crying and started shouting. Appa laughed out loud and hugged me with muddy hands. Salim anna took his magnet back, wiped it on his shirt and looked at it as if he had never seen it before.

After dinner, I went round the kitchen with Amma's fridge magnet. It stuck to the tawa, the steel almirah and the gas cylinder. It did not stick to the brass diya, the copper pot or the aluminium pan. It slid off my steel tumbler, but it held on to my steel spoon.
On Monday, Salim anna came down the lane again. He stopped at our gate and held up his magnet. 'So, Meena,' he said. 'Did you ask your teacher yet?'
item.epiphany: For the parent: the turn is when the magnet keeps coming up empty. Appa thinks the water is stopping the magnet. Meena remembers that the magnet slid off the brass lota but stuck to the steel lid. She realises the keys are brass, which a magnet does not attract, but the small ring is steel, which it does. The story also shows the magnet jumping across a gap to the iron grating, and acting through water. Let your child find these out in the tests on Days 1 to 3 before you name them.
ask: Why did Salim anna's magnet stick to the cooker lid but not to the lota?
Why did the magnet jump sideways onto the drain grating?
Appa thought the water was stopping the magnet. How could we test whether he was right?
Why did Meena aim the magnet at the ring and not at the keys?
Meena's magnet slid off her steel tumbler but held her steel spoon. What could that mean?

item.title: The settling jar
item.question: What is soil made of, and how can we find the clay in it?
need: a clear glass jar or plastic bottle with a lid
3 big spoons of soil from a plant pot or tree bed (not cocopeat)
steps: Put 3 big spoons of soil in the jar.
Fill the jar two-thirds with water and close the lid tightly.
Shake hard for one minute.
Put it down where nobody will move it, and watch for 2 minutes.
Look again the next day and draw the layers.
item.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'If we leave it still, what will happen to the soil? Will it all sink at the same speed?'
item.observe: In a minute, gritty sand is at the bottom. Over some hours a finer layer of silt settles on it, then a thin, smooth layer of clay. The water above can stay cloudy for a day or more.
item.why: Soil is a mix of grains of different sizes. Big, heavy sand grains sink fast. Silt grains are smaller and sink more slowly. Clay grains are so tiny you cannot see one, so they sink slowest of all, and some stay floating. Potters clean clay the same way: they mix soil with water, let the sand sink, and take the fine clay from the top.
item.safety: Wash hands after touching soil. Keep the jar where it will not fall.
item.time: 5 min + look again the next day

item.who: Salim Ali (1896–1987), bird scientist, India
item.idea: Salim Ali was one of the first scientists to study Indian birds by watching them alive, for long hours, instead of only collecting dead ones. In 1931 he published a careful study of how baya weavers nest. He described the males weaving nests and the females visiting half-built nests and choosing among them.
item.then: At the time, most bird study in India meant shooting birds and describing their bodies. Patient watching of how birds behave was rare.
item.now: Later studies agree that male bayas build and females choose. Why bayas press small lumps of mud inside their nests is still not settled.
item.ask: Salim Ali learned by watching the same birds again and again. What could you find out about the crows or pigeons near your home just by watching every day for a week?

item.who: The seamstresses of the International Latex Corporation (ILC), Dover, Delaware, USA (1960s)
item.idea: The company, until then best known for making bras and girdles, won the job of making the Apollo moon suits. Its seamstresses, mostly women, sewed many layers of different materials, each with a job, to extremely exact measurements. Even pins were banned in case one pierced the airtight layer.
item.then: Few people outside the factory knew their names. The suits were credited to the company and the engineers, and the astronauts became famous.
item.now: Historians, for example Nicholas de Monchaux in his book 'Spacesuit: Fashioning Apollo', have written about how much the suits depended on the seamstresses' skill. Every suit that walked on the Moon worked.
item.ask: Why do you think the skill of sewing was not seen as 'science'? What would have happened to the astronauts without it?

item.title: What does Teddy see?
item.question: Can you work out what someone else sees from where they sit?
need: a ball, a thick book and a steel tumbler
steps: Your child sits on one side of the table. Put the soft toy on a chair on the other side, facing your child.
In the middle, put the book standing up, the tumbler in front of it on your child's side, and the ball behind it on Teddy's side.
Without moving, your child draws what Teddy sees: which things, and which is in front.
Your child walks round, crouches behind Teddy and looks. Was the drawing right?
Swap the toy to the side of the table and try again.
item.predict: Ask: 'Will Teddy's picture look the same as yours? What will Teddy see that you can't?'
item.observe: From Teddy's seat, the ball is in front and the tumbler is hidden behind the book, the opposite of your child's view.
item.why: Each person sees from the place where they are. To know what someone else sees, you must imagine yourself in their place. The scientist Jean Piaget thought children under about seven could not do this. Later, the psychologist Martin Hughes gave young children a version that made sense to them, hiding a doll from toy policemen. Most four-year-olds solved it. Seeing from another point of view grows early, and we can keep getting better at it.

item.title: The people survey
need: a table drawn on paper with 6 columns
a hard book to write on
at least 8 people, in person or on a video call
steps: Draw a table with these columns: name, eye colour, which hand they write with, first language, favourite fruit, height.
Ask each person the questions and fill one row. Look at eye colour in good light.
Measure heights for the people at home. Each person stands against a wall without chappals. Put a book flat on their head, mark the wall, and measure from the floor to the mark.
Write heights in metres and centimetres. For example, 1 metre 21 centimetres is 1.21 m.
Keep the table safe. You need it on Day 4 and for the project.
item.outcome: A table of data about at least 8 people.

item.who: Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose, officers of the Bengal Police, Kolkata, India, in the 1890s
item.idea: In the 1890s, the two officers worked for Edward Henry, the head of the Bengal Police, on a way to sort fingerprint cards. Haque worked out much of the counting that splits the cards into groups by the pattern on each finger. Bose added ways to sort them further. With their method, one card could be found quickly among many thousands.
item.then: The method was taken up across British India in 1897 and by Scotland Yard in London in 1901. It was named the Henry system, after their boss. For many years, the usual story left out Haque and Bose.
item.now: Historians now agree that Haque and Bose did key parts of the work. Some people now call it the Henry, Haque and Bose system.
item.ask: Who usually gets the credit: the person who does the work, or the person in charge? How could we find out who really did the work?

item.who: Richard Lewontin (1929–2021), USA, geneticist
item.idea: In 1972 Lewontin measured how much people differ in some of their genes. He compared people from the same group with people from different parts of the world. He found that about 85% of the differences were between people of the same group. Only a small share was between groups.
item.then: Many people had thought humans could be sorted into a few separate groups by skin colour, like boxes. Lewontin's result showed the boxes do not match the genes.
item.now: Many later studies with much more data found the same pattern. The scientist A. W. F. Edwards pointed out in 2003 that, if you look at many genes together, you can often tell where a person's ancestors came from. Both are true. Features change gradually across the world, and most of the differences are still between people of the same group.
item.ask: Two children from the same city, and two children from different countries. Which two will differ more? How could you test it?

item.who: Nina Jablonski and George Chaplin, USA, scientists who study human evolution
item.idea: In 2000 Jablonski and Chaplin compared skin colour with the amount of UV sunlight in each part of the world. Skin is darker where UV is strongest, near the equator, and lighter where it is weak. Their explanation: melanin protects the body from strong UV. But skin also needs some UV to make vitamin D, which keeps bones strong. So where sunlight is weak, lighter skin helps.
item.then: Earlier scientists had noticed the link with sunlight, but Jablonski and Chaplin measured it across the world and explained both sides of the balance.
item.now: Most scientists accept that sunlight shaped skin colour. Details are still studied, such as how food rich in vitamin D, like fish, changed things for some people in the far north.
item.ask: Your skin colour came from where your ancestors lived for thousands of years. Does it tell you anything about what you are like inside?

item.who: John Marzluff, University of Washington, USA, crow scientist
item.idea: In 2006 Marzluff and his students wore a rubber caveman mask while they caught and ringed a few crows, then let them go unharmed. Afterwards, whenever anyone walked through that place in the mask, crows scolded them with loud caws and swooped at them. People in other masks were left alone. Crows that had never been caught, and young crows born later, joined in.
item.then: Before this, few scientists had tested whether wild birds know individual human faces.
item.now: The study was published in 2010. Crows kept scolding the mask for years. Crows recognise individual human faces, and they learn from each other which faces are dangerous.
item.ask: Why might telling human faces apart matter more to a crow than telling crows apart matters to us?

item.title: The mirror tunnel
item.question: If two mirrors face each other, do the reflections go on for ever?
need: a wall mirror or dressing-table mirror
a small hand mirror (or the mirror from a make-up compact)
steps: Stand in front of the big mirror. Hold the small mirror just under your eyes, facing the big mirror.
Tilt the small mirror a little until you see a tunnel of mirrors inside mirrors.
Count how many copies of the mirror you can see. Count two more times and write down all three counts.
Look at the far copies. Are they as bright as the near ones? What colour are they?
Swap, so the other person holds the mirror and counts.
item.predict: Ask: 'How many copies will you see? Will they go on for ever? Why do you think so?'
item.observe: You see a line of mirrors, each smaller than the one before. You can often count 10 or more. The far copies are dimmer and look a little green, and then the tunnel fades away. The tunnel often curves, because the mirrors are not exactly facing each other.
item.why: Light bounces from one mirror to the other again and again. Each copy is the light after one more bounce. At every bounce the mirror soaks up a little of the light, so each copy is dimmer than the last. The glass of a mirror soaks up a little more red light than green light, so the far copies look green. After enough bounces, too little light is left to see. Perfect mirrors could keep the tunnel going much longer, but no real mirror is perfect.
item.safety: Hold glass mirrors carefully with both hands. Never point a mirror at the Sun.

item.title: Listening to nothing
steps: Sit cross-legged on the floor, back straight, hands on your knees. Close your eyes.
For one minute, stay as still as a statue and listen. Make no sound.
Open your eyes. Write down every sound you heard: a fan, a horn, a bird, your own breathing.
Clap this rhythm together: clap, clap, rest, clap. On the rest, open your hands without a sound. Repeat it 4 times.
Draw the rhythm in the notebook: a dot for each clap, a 0 for each rest.
Your child makes up a rhythm with one rest, and then one with three rests. Clap both. Ask which one sounds more different.
item.outcome: A list of the sounds in a 'silent' minute, and two rhythms written with 0s for the rests.

lessons.title: Patterns and symmetry: flip it, turn it, slide it

flagged.item: translation: patterns that repeat by sliding

item: a flip, like the picture in a mirror. Left and right swap over.
a slide. The shape moves along without turning or flipping.
shapes that fit together with no gaps and no overlaps, like floor tiles

item.who: Dan Shechtman (born 1941), materials scientist, Israel
item.idea: On 8 April 1982, Shechtman cooled a melted mix of aluminium and manganese very fast and looked at it with an electron microscope. The picture showed spots that looked the same after each tenth of a turn. That meant its atoms were ordered with five-fold symmetry, like a five-pointed star. A crystal's repeating pattern can never have five-fold symmetry, so this should have been impossible. He wrote 'ten-fold???' in his notebook.
item.then: Many scientists said he had made a mistake, and he was asked to leave his research group. Linus Pauling, a famous chemist, argued against him for years.
item.now: Other laboratories made the same material and saw the same pattern. These solids are called quasicrystals: ordered patterns that never repeat. In 1992 the definition of a crystal was changed to include them, and Shechtman won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011.
item.ask: Shechtman's result broke a rule everybody trusted. When should a scientist trust a new result over an old rule?

item.who: Bhushan Karihaloo, engineer at Cardiff University, Wales, and the honeycomb debate
item.idea: In 2013 Karihaloo and his colleagues looked at new honeycomb cells. They said bees first build round cells. The bees' body warmth softens the wax, and where three walls meet, the soft wax pulls itself straight, as soap films do. So the hexagons form by themselves.
item.then: About 1,700 years ago the Greek mathematician Pappus wrote that bees choose the hexagon because it holds the most honey for the least wax. In 1999 the mathematician Thomas Hales proved that a pattern of hexagons divides a flat space into equal cells with the least total wall.
item.now: Other scientists filmed and measured bees at work. They argue that the bees shape the hexagons themselves, using their bodies and jaws, and feel the wall thickness as they build. Both groups agree hexagons use the least wax. They still argue about how the bees make them.
item.ask: If the wax shapes itself, are the bees still the builders? What would you need to watch to decide?

item.author: Loreen Leedy

item.who: Monica Gagliano (born 1976), Australia, and her critics
item.idea: In 2014 Gagliano reported that touch-me-not plants dropped harmlessly again and again stopped folding their leaves, and 'remembered' this for weeks, which she called learning.
item.then: Some plant scientists praised the experiment. Others said words like 'learning' and 'intelligence' should be kept for animals with nervous systems, and that other explanations had not been ruled out.
item.now: Plants sense, remember and respond, as this experiment shows. Scientists still argue about whether to call it learning and intelligence, or to keep those words for animals with nerves.
item.ask: What would a plant have to do for you to call it clever?

item.author: Robin Wall Kimmerer, adapted by Monique Gray Smith
item.why: A botanist from the Potawatomi Nation on seeing plants as relatives and teachers. Read short sections aloud and talk.

lessons.title: How temperature changes the way seeds sprout and plants grow

item.who: Yasuyuki Aono, Osaka Prefecture University, Japan, and the people of Kyoto who kept the record
item.idea: Aono gathered the dates when Kyoto's cherry trees reached full bloom, from court diaries, poems and temple records going back to the 9th century, making one of the longest records of nature on Earth. It shows bloom dates getting earlier in modern times as springs warm. In 2021 the trees peaked on 26 March, the earliest in about 1,200 years of records.
item.then: For centuries, the dates were written for festivals and poetry, not for science. Nobody knew they would one day be evidence.
item.now: Scientists accept that warmer springs make many plants flower earlier around the world. The Kyoto record is used as evidence of warming, alongside thermometers. It reminds us that people who weren't called scientists made the data.
item.ask: What could you write down every year, starting now, that a scientist in 300 years might thank you for?

lessons.title: Senses: how the body picks up the world and the brain makes a picture of it

item.title: Siddhesh in the Dark
text: My brother Siddhesh is eleven and he can do things on a wooden pole that would make a monkey nervous. The pole is called a mallakhamb. It stands in the sand pit behind a gymnasium near Shivaji Park in Dadar, taller than our father, smooth and oiled and shining, and every evening for three years Siddhesh has climbed it, wrapped himself round it, hung from it by one foot, and made shapes on it like a peacock, a bow, a flag in the wind.
I am seven. I sit on the bench with our coach's water bottle and watch.
Our coach is called Tai. She is small and grey-haired and she has been training mallakhamb children since before our parents were born. Tai never shouts. She just says, “Again,” and you do it again.
Last winter, at the district competition, Siddhesh fell.

It wasn't a big fall. He was halfway through the peacock, where you hold yourself out sideways from the pole with your legs, and he looked down at the crowd. There were hundreds of people on the benches, waving and moving and clapping, and the lights were in his eyes. He told me later that the whole crowd seemed to slide sideways, like the sea. His body thought it was falling. So it fell.
He landed on his feet in the sand, but he lost. And after that, every time he climbed the pole, he looked down and froze.
One evening Tai took the cloth she wipes the pole with, folded it, and tied it over his eyes.
“How can I do it if I can't see?” he said.
“Your eyes lied to you,” said Tai. “The crowd moved and your eyes told you that you were moving. Your eyes are good for many things. But up there you have two other friends who never lie.”
She tapped him behind his ear. “One lives in here. Three small tubes of water inside your ear. When you tip, the water tips. It tells you which way is down even in the dark.”

She tapped his arm, his knee, his ankle. “The other lives everywhere. In every muscle and every joint. It tells you where your arm is, and how bent your knee is, without looking. Shut your eyes and touch your nose.”
He did, easily.
“How did you find your nose?” said Tai. “You did not see it.”
Siddhesh didn't answer. I could see him thinking.
“Again,” said Tai.

That first evening blindfolded, he could hardly get off the ground. He felt for the pole with his hands like an old man feeling for a door in the dark. He slipped and slid and banged his chin. I wanted to take the cloth off him. Tai shook her head at me.

But the next week he could climb. The week after, he could hold the bow. By spring he could do the whole routine with his eyes covered, slowly, every shape, and when he came down he was smiling in a way he hadn't smiled since the fall.
“What does it feel like?” I asked him on the way home.
He thought about it. “Like the pole is part of me,” he said. “Like I'm listening to my arms.”
This year, at the district competition, it was very hot and there were even more people. Siddhesh was the last to go. He chalked his hands, climbed up, and began.
He was halfway through the peacock when every light in the hall went out.

It was a power cut, the kind we have all the time in summer, but in the middle of a crowd it was terrifying. Total dark. People screamed. Somewhere a baby cried. I grabbed the edge of the bench and thought of my brother, three metres up a pole, sideways, in the black.
Then people began to switch on their phone torches, one by one, and pointed them at the pole.
Siddhesh was still there.

He was holding the peacock, his body out flat from the pole, perfectly still, as if nothing had happened. In the shaky light of a hundred phones, he came out of the peacock and moved into the bow, and then the flag, every shape in order, slowly, the way he had done it in the evenings with Tai's cloth over his eyes. The crowd went completely quiet. The only sound was the wood creaking under his hands.
When he slid down into the sand, the lights came back on, and the noise was so loud I had to cover my ears.
He didn't win, actually. He came second, because the judges said they couldn't see his first shape properly. He didn't mind. On the way home I asked him if he'd been scared when the lights went out.
“For one second,” he said. “Then I remembered I wasn't using them.”
Tai was walking with us. She didn't say anything. She just put her hand on top of his head for a moment, and then took it away.
item.epiphany: We have senses beyond the five: balance (from the fluid in the inner ear) and proprioception (from receptors in muscles and joints, telling us where our body is), and the eyes can even mislead them, as when the moving crowd makes Siddhesh feel he is falling. The turn is the power cut: everyone else is blind, but Siddhesh carries on because he has trained to use the senses that do not need light.
ask: Why did Siddhesh fall the first time?
What were the 'two friends who never lie' that Tai talked about? What are their real names?
How did Siddhesh touch his nose without seeing it?
Why could he keep going when the lights went out?
Siddhesh said he was 'listening to his arms'. What do you think he meant? Try it.

item.who: Kinji Imanishi (1902–1992) and the Koshima monkey watchers, Japan
item.idea: Imanishi and his students at Kyoto University watched wild Japanese macaques for many years. He argued that animals can have culture: habits learned from each other, not born in them. In 1953 on Koshima island, a young female they named Imo began washing sweet potatoes in water. Satsue Mito, a local woman who helped the scientists watch the monkeys, was among the first to record it. A playmate copied her first, then her mother, and the habit spread through the group over years. Old males were slowest to learn.
item.then: Many scientists in Europe and America said culture belonged to humans only, and that the Japanese scientists were too ready to see minds in animals.
item.now: Today many scientists agree that some animals have traditions passed on by learning: chimpanzees cracking nuts with stones, whales singing songs, macaques washing food. How alike these are to human culture is still argued about.
item.ask: What would you need to see to be sure a habit was learned by watching, and not born in the animal?

item.title: The mystery dabbas
item.question: Can we find something hidden without seeing it, just by what it does?
need: 2 identical steel dabbas or tiffin boxes with lids
a 500 g packet of dal wrapped in a cloth so it doesn't rattle
steps: Before the lesson, a grown-up hides the dal packet in one dabba and closes both. Your child must not open them.
Test 1: put both dabbas on the floor. Your child pushes each one slowly across the floor with one finger. Which one is harder to push?
Test 2: put each dabba in a cloth bag or knot it in a handkerchief. Hang each bag from a rubber band, holding the top of the band. Which band stretches more?
Your child says which dabba has the hidden weight, and gives the reason from both tests.
Open both dabbas and check.
item.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'Both dabbas look exactly the same. How could you find out which one has something heavy inside, without opening it?'
item.observe: The heavy dabba is harder to push, and it stretches its rubber band more. Both tests point to the same dabba.
item.why: We could not see the dal, but we could see what its mass did. It made the dabba harder to move, and it pulled down more. Astronomers find dark matter in the same way. They cannot see it, but they see stars going round galaxies too fast, and light bending round galaxy clusters. Something with mass must be there, adding gravity.
item.safety: Keep the stretched rubber band away from faces, in case it snaps.

item.who: Paul Dirac (1902–1984), England, and Carl Anderson (1905–1991), United States
item.idea: In 1928, Dirac found an equation for the electron. It also allowed a particle just like the electron but with a plus charge. In 1931 he said this anti-electron should really exist. In 1932, Anderson photographed its track in a cloud chamber, among particles coming from space, and named it the positron.
item.then: Many physicists thought the extra answers in Dirac's maths were a mistake. Dirac himself first guessed they might be protons. Anderson's photograph settled it.
item.now: Antimatter is real and well tested. Hospitals use positrons in PET scans, and scientists at CERN in Switzerland have made and trapped atoms of antihydrogen. Why the universe has so much more matter than antimatter is still unknown.
item.ask: Dirac's maths predicted a particle nobody had seen. Would you have believed it before Anderson's photograph? What would you need to see?

item.title: The neuron squeeze
steps: Everyone sits in a line holding hands. Each person is a neuron, and each pair of joined hands is a synapse.
The first person starts the timer and squeezes the next person's hand. Each person squeezes the next as soon as they feel it. The last person says 'Done!'.
Time it. Do it three times. Does it get faster with practice?
Now try passing the message by saying 'go' instead of squeezing. Faster or slower?
Ask: 'In the real body, messages travel up to about 100 metres a second in the fastest nerves. How long would our message take if each of us was a real neuron?' (A tiny fraction of a second.)
item.outcome: A felt sense that messages travel from neuron to neuron, and that practice makes the chain faster.

item.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858–1937), India, and Toshiyuki Nakagaki, Japan
item.idea: From about 1900 to 1920, Bose built very sensitive instruments, like his crescograph. He showed that plants respond to touch, heat and chemicals with electrical signals, and that anaesthetics dull those responses, as they do in animals. In 2000, Nakagaki and colleagues put a slime mould in a maze, with food at two exits. A slime mould is one giant cell with no brain or neurons. It grew along the shortest route between the two foods.
item.then: Bose's electrical measurements impressed scientists, but his claims that plants have something like feelings or a nervous system were widely doubted. Nakagaki's maze result was published in the journal Nature and was widely reported.
item.now: Both findings are accepted. Plants do signal with electricity, and slime moulds do solve such problems. Scientists such as Michael Levin and Pamela Lyon show that sensing, deciding and remembering began in single cells, long before neurons. They call it basal cognition. Other scientists keep the words thinking and memory for animals with nerves. A slime mould is not a fungus or a bacterium. It is a living thing of its own kind.
item.ask: A slime mould with no brain solved a maze. What did it have to sense and decide to do that?

item.who: Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, USA (1999)
item.idea: In 1999 Simons and Chabris asked people to watch a short film of players passing basketballs and count the passes made by one team. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks into the middle, thumps their chest and walks off. About half the viewers didn't notice the gorilla at all.
item.then: The result surprised many people, including psychologists, and became one of the most famous experiments about attention, called 'inattentional blindness'.
item.now: It has been repeated many times, in many versions. It shows that attention is limited and that we are often unaware of what we miss, and it matters for things like road safety (drivers who are busy with phones miss people crossing). How many people miss it depends on how hard the task is.
item.ask: If you can miss a gorilla, what else might you be missing right now? How would you ever find out?

item.who: Clair Patterson (1922–1995), geochemist, USA
item.idea: In the 1950s Patterson measured the age of the Earth, about 4.5 billion years. To do it he had to measure tiny amounts of lead, and he found lead everywhere. He showed that lead in the air, the sea and people's bodies had shot up in modern times. Most of it came from lead that was added to petrol, starting in the 1920s.
item.then: Oil and lead companies, and scientists paid by them, said the lead was natural and harmless. Patterson lost some of his research money, and was kept off a 1971 national committee on lead in the air.
item.now: He was right. Even small amounts of lead harm children's brains. Countries began banning leaded petrol in the 1970s. India stopped selling it in 2000, and the last country stopped in 2021. Lead in people's blood has fallen sharply.
item.ask: Patterson compared old ice from deep in Greenland with new ice near the top. The new ice had far more lead. Why was comparing old and new such strong evidence?

item.who: Samuel Morse (1791–1872) and Alfred Vail (1807–1859), USA
item.idea: Morse was a painter who began working on an electric telegraph in the 1830s. Alfred Vail joined him in 1837. He and his family put money into the work, and he built much of the machinery. On 24 May 1844, Morse sent the first message on a long telegraph line, from Washington to Baltimore, and Vail received it.
item.then: Morse got the fame and most of the money. The dot-and-dash code was named after him.
item.now: Historians still argue about who made the code for the letters. Morse's first plan was to send numbers that stood for words in a code book. Some historians think Vail worked out the letter code, using short codes for common letters like E and T. Others think Morse did. Vail's own papers do not settle it.
item.ask: Vail built the machines and may have made the code, but the code has Morse's name. What evidence would you want to see before deciding who made it?

item.who: Ignaz Semmelweis (1818–1865), doctor, Hungary and Austria
item.idea: In 1847, at a big hospital in Vienna, many mothers were dying of a fever soon after giving birth. Semmelweis saw that doctors often came straight from cutting open dead bodies to help mothers give birth. He made the doctors wash their hands in a chlorine solution first. Far fewer mothers died.
item.then: Many doctors were offended at the idea that their own hands were making mothers ill. Nobody yet knew that germs cause disease, so he could not explain what was being carried. He lost his job in Vienna. He died in 1865, in an asylum, of an infected wound.
item.now: In the years after he died, scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that germs cause disease. Semmelweis was right. Handwashing is now one of the most important ways to stop illness.
item.ask: Semmelweis had good results, but he could not see or show the thing that was harming people. What would you need to see before you believed in something invisible?
